en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Oṃ. Now.
At its commencement, its course, and its cessation, there are drops of the flowing ichor of pride.
I bow to that elephant-faced one, who is the cause of the phenomenal world. (1)
I worship the pair of lotus feet of the Lord Saccidānanda.
By the upward lift of whose glance for a moment, I, Śiva, perform the five cosmic acts. (2)
In the first stage of departure, she is of the nature of light; in the second, she rains down death.
And on the path of my return journey, I worship the digit of consciousness within the Unmanifest. (3)
Having thoroughly examined all the Tantras, including those pertaining to Yama, without exception.
Having understood from the mouth of the Guru their secret meanings according to reality. (4)
A bee at the pair of lotus feet of the Lord who is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss.
I am Śrīvidyānandanātha, free from passion and possessed of discerning wisdom. (5)
Wandering over this earth together with wise men of pure soul.
He was entreated at Prayāga for their pleasure and for the welfare of the world. (6)
It has the five streams as its water and is filled with the jewels of those mantras.
The entire circle of yoginīs is radiant like a coral creeper. (7)
It is expanded by the mass of moonlight from the full moon of the eternal maṇḍala.
The great island of nine wheels, with its internal waves of the network of ritual placements. (8)
The boat of the sandals of Śrīnātha, which is the nectar of the fruit of the four aims of life.
I shall reveal very clearly the Jewel-Mine of Good Fortune. (9)
The daily and occasional worship of Śrīvidyā, along with its various divisions.
The worship for specific desires and the practice of the eastern direction and so forth are constituent parts of initiation. (10)
The varieties of initiation, the preliminary rites, and the rules for those rituals and so forth.
And the procedure for optional oblations, according to the distinction between gentle and cruel [deities]. (11)
From the recitation of the Vidyā, both in its entirety and in its parts, the arising of desired fruits occurs.
And the rules of right conduct and so forth are likewise written down in this ocean of jewels. (12)

There, at the third watch of the night, the illustrious practitioner should wake up, perform his necessary duties, wash his hands and feet, put on two clean garments, sip water for purification, and sit upon his seat.
Having removed the floral remains from the image of the deity, he should [proceed] with the flowers and other materials remaining from the previous day’s worship.
Having worshipped with the collective vidyā beginning with "samasta-prakaṭa" which will be described hereafter,
[one should meditate on the Lord] seated upon a throne in the pericarp of the white thousand-petaled lotus situated in the *brahmarandhra*,
together with the Goddess resting upon his left side.

Having meditated upon the venerable Guru in the form of Śiva—adorned with red garments, ornaments, garlands, and unguents; resembling a moonstone; possessing three eyes; holding the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), a book, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; peaceful and most gracious—one should [bathe] one’s own body with the streams of nectar flowing from the pair of his lotus feet.

Having visualized [the deity] as being completely immersed, one should utter the three essences of the *praṇava*, and at the end of the *Śrīgurupādukā-vidyā* to be described hereafter, worship with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), saying: "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Śrī-Amukānandanātha. Then, one should recite the hymn (*stotra*).
It is as follows:
One should daily praise him with these five verses for the sake of all accomplishments.
By reciting [this] at the time of awakening in the morning, the day shall become auspicious. (1)
Salutations to you, O Lord, Blessed One, Śiva in the form of the Guru.
O you who have assumed many forms for the sake of the successful entry into knowledge! (2)
To the ever-new one, whose form is ever-new, who illuminates the ultimate truth.
To you, the mass of consciousness, who are like the sun that shatters the darkness of all ignorance. (3)
To the independent one, whose form is fashioned by compassion, the very self of Śiva.
To the one who is dependent on others, to the devotees, to those destined for liberation, and to the one whose form is auspiciousness. (4)
For the sake of discernment by those who possess discernment, and for the sake of investigation by those who investigate.
To the light of lights, to the one whose form is knowledge for the wise. (5)
I shall pay homage in front, at the sides, behind, above, and below.
Always, by means of your own form as my mind, fashion a seat for me. (6)
O Lord, by your grace, I am forever one who has accomplished his purpose.
I am liberated from the great noose of illusory death; I am Śiva here. (7)
Having thus prostrated.
Beginning in the morning and ending at evening, or beginning at evening and continuing until morning.
O Lord of the World, whatever I do, let that be an offering unto You. (8)
Having thus offered [it].
One should contemplate dissolution into one's own heart with the heart-mantra; thus, having performed the meditation on the Guru.

Having meditated upon a yellow four-petalled lotus at one's own *mūlādhāra*, encircled by a square and endowed with the four letters beginning with *va* and ending with *sa*, one should visualize within its pericarp a triangular *kula-śṛṅgāṭa* consisting of three lines representing the Moon, Sun, and Fire, originating from the letters *a*, *ka*, and *tha*; and in the center of that, ten million suns.

Having meditated upon the Bindu named Kāma— which resembles ten million moons, is exceedingly cool, possesses the radiance of a Japā flower, and is permeated by the qualities of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas— one should then contemplate above it the Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpa), who is endowed with thirty-eight Kalās, and whose body consists of the fifty letters.

Having visualized her as the embodiment of Śrīvidyā, blazing with the brilliance of ten million lightning bolts, thinner than a lotus fiber, like a sleeping serpent, situated with three-and-a-half coils,
and having struck her with the pure stalk [of the central channel], one should raise her by means of the Suṣumṇā path from the Mūlādhāra according to the method taught by the Guru.

Having reached the thousand-petalled lotus situated at the *brahmarandhra* by means of the sequence of piercing the six chakras known as Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā, one should then satisfy that Kuṇḍalinī with a stream of red-colored nectar flowing from there— consisting of the phonemes— and once again [with] the stream of nectar.

Having brought [the breath], which possesses its own form and is unmanifest (akula), along with the boat of nectar, through the sequence of the Ājñā, Viśuddha, and other centers down to the Mūlādhāra— flooding each respective support, element, syllable, and presiding deity within the Suṣumṇā— in that very same manner...
One should establish [the deity] by meditating on the supreme power Kuṇḍalinī according to the sequence of ascent and descent.
One should meditate on the three peaks of the Vidyā.
There, having visualized the fire-mandala consisting of ten digits at the *mūlādhāra*,

one should visualize there the first syllable-cluster (*kūṭa*) of the root-mantra, known as *vāgbhava*, which is radiant like a flashing streak of lightning, reaching as far as the *anāhata* [cakra], with its crest of sound (*nādaśikha*) having reached that *anāhata*.

Having meditated upon the solar disc consisting of twelve kalās, one should meditate within its center upon the second *kūṭa* of the root-mantra known as Kāmarāja— which resembles the rising sun, reaches up to the *ājñā*-cakra, possesses a crest of *nāda*, and has rays extending upwards and downwards— within the *ājñā*-cakra.

Having meditated upon the lunar mandala consisting of sixteen digits, one should meditate in its center on the third peak (kūṭa) of the root-mantra, known as Śakti, which resembles the full moon, reaches up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), has a crest of resonance (nāda-śikhā) extending there, and has rays streaming downward and upward. Then...
Having meditated upon the Root Mantra (Mūlavidyā) as a single, unbroken column of light, radiant as a thousand rising suns, extending from the Mūlādhāra to the Brahma-randhra;
and having contemplated one's own body as pervaded by that light, [one should meditate] upon the venerable Supreme Deity, who is transformed by that light, within the lotus of the heart.
Having meditated and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra,

perform the aforementioned nyāsas of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth along with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of the root mantra, recite the root mantra as many times as possible, and having recited it, offer the recitation (japa).
At dawn, I bow to the lotus feet of the Mother of the worlds.
To the illustrious Tripurasundarī, who is bowed down to by Hara and the other gods; (1)
In the morning, I bow to the lotus feet of Tripurasundarī.
By her, Hari, Hara, and Viriñci perform the acts of creation and the rest. (2)
In the morning, I bow to the lotus feet of Tripurasundarī.
The Gaṅgā shines upon the head of Maheśvara, the source of all that has been done. (3)
In the morning, I bow to her who holds a noose, a goad, an arrow, and a bow in her hands.
The illustrious Tripurasundarī, who resembles the rising sun. (4)
At dawn, I bow to the lotus-feet by which this entire world is illumined.
By whose grace one turns back from that [cycle] of Tripurasundarī. (5)
The man who recites these five verses every morning regularly, [attains...]
To him, Śrī Tripurasundarī shall grant her own abode. (6)
Having thus praised and prostrated before her, one should announce one's own task.
It is as follows:
Having thus offered [the ritual], one should pray for the command of the Goddess in order to perform one's own duties.
Namely as follows:
O Sovereign of the lords, whose very essence is the consciousness of the three worlds, O Śrī Sundarī, it is solely by the command of Your feet [that this has come to pass].
Having risen early in the morning, for the sake of your pleasure, I desire to follow the course of worldly life. (1)
O Śrī Tripurā, Supreme Goddess, by your command, I shall follow the course of this journey through saṃsāra.
O Mother, may rivalry, contempt, strife, negligence, and fear overcome me. (2)
I know the Dharma, yet I have no engagement in it; I know the Dharma, yet I have no withdrawal from it.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, I abide within your heart; I shall do exactly as I am commanded. (3)

Thus, having requested the command of the Goddess, and reflecting, "I am proceeding by means of some play of consciousness (*cidvilāsa*) in which all adventitious limitations (*upādhi*) have been cast off, preceded by the contemplation of the *nāda* (the primordial sound) according to the path taught by my own guru," one should, for the sake of performing one's own ritual duties, [realize] the innate (*sahaja*) [nature] known through the guru’s instruction.
Having accomplished the silent recitation (ajapājapa), one should offer it to the respective deities.
It is as follows:
O Argha, on the previous day,

one performs the *ajapā-japa*— consisting of inhalations and exhalations numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred— which has been recited throughout the day and night, at the *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and *maṇipūra*.
The unstruck [sound] is purified through the centers known as the *ājñā*,

situated within the four-petaled, six-petaled, ten-petaled, twelve-petaled, sixteen-petaled, two-petaled, and thousand-petaled lotuses at the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), which possess the colors of gold, coral, blue, tawny, smoke-colored, lightning, and camphor.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), saying: "I shall offer this to Gaṇapati, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the individual self (*jīvātman*), the supreme self (*paramātman*), and the sandals of the venerable Guru (*śrīgurupādukā*), each according to its respective portion," he should then perform the offering.
It is as follows:
Oṃ aiṃ hīṃ śrīṃ. I offer six hundred ajapā recitations to Gaṇapati residing at the mūlādhāra; salutations. (4)
I offer six thousand ajapā-japas to Viṣṇu residing in the maṇipūraka-cakra, and to Brahmā residing in the svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra; obeisance! (4)
I offer six thousand ajapā-japas to Viṣṇu, who resides in the maṇipūraka-cakra; obeisance. (4)
I offer six thousand ajapā-japas to Rudra, who resides in the Anāhata Cakra; salutations.
I offer one thousand ajapā-japas to the Jīvātman, who resides in the Viśuddha Cakra; salutations. I offer one thousand ajapā-japas to the Paramātman, who resides in the Ājñā Cakra; salutations.
(Thus one should offer. To perform this much:
"I offer a thousand repetitions of the *ajapā* to the sandals of the venerable Guru residing in the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus; obeisance. Thus one should offer.
If one is unable to do this much— (4) ||

I offer this Ajapā-japa, numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred, consisting of inhalations and exhalations uttered by me during the preceding day and night, to the Śrī-guru-pādukā residing in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus situated in the Brahma-randhra; obeisance! Thus, [this is] indeed for the Gurus.
One should offer it.
Having thus offered the merit of the recitation (*japa*), [one says]: *Oṃ*.

"Beginning from today at sunrise, for one full day and night, I shall perform the *ajapā-japa* consisting of inhalation and exhalation, numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred times. Thus, with palms joined in reverence.
Having formed the mental resolve.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the Ajapā mantra, [one should place] "Haṃsāya ṛṣaye namaḥ" on the head.

In the mouth (4): Salutation to the unmanifest Gāyatrī metre. In the heart (4): Salutation to the Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa) deity. At the Mūlādhāra (4): Salutation to the seed-syllable *Haṃ*. In the two feet (4): Salutation to the power (*Śakti*) *Saḥ*.
At the navel: (4) sohaṃ kīlakāya namaḥ.
In the heart: *oṃ* to Oṃkāra, the principle, obeisance. In the head: *na* to Nabhas, the station, obeisance.
To the golden-colored one on all limbs, salutation. To the acute accent as sound on the throat, salutation.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should speak with palms joined in reverence: "The application (*viniyoga*) is for my recitation (*japa*) for the sake of liberation."
Then, on the two thumbs: Oṃ (3) hsāṃ, svāhā to the self of the Sun; obeisance to the heart.
On the two index fingers: (4) *hsī* to the self that is Soma, *svāhā*; to the head, *svāhā*.
In the two middle [fingers] (4): *hsūṃ* to the stainless self, *svāhā*; to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*.
To the two ring fingers, *hseṃ* to the one whose nature is free from appearances, *svāhā*; to the armor, *huṃ*.
On the two little fingers (4) *hsauṃ*: "O infinite-bodied one, O subtle one, impel the Self! Svāhā!"—*vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes.
On the palms and backs of the hands: (4) *hsaḥ* svāhā to the unmanifest self of consciousness; *phaṭ* to the weapon.
Having thus placed [the mantras] on the two hands,
one should likewise place these same mantras on the six limbs, beginning with the heart.
One should practice meditation. It is as follows:
The wise declare Him whose head is the earth, whose navel is the sky, and whose two eyes are the moon and the sun.
He whose ears are the quarters of space and whose feet are the earth—he, the inner self of all beings, is to be meditated upon. (1)
The Self is not possessed of the two wings called Agni and Soma; it is of the nature of Śiva.
It exits through the letter *ha* and enters through the letter *sa*. (2)
Having remembered "I am that Haṃsa," one becomes "so'ham" (that-I) when deprived of the consonant.
Having withdrawn the wings, one should visualize oneself in the form of an egg. (3)
Thus, having meditated upon one's own self as the nature of Virāṭ and having contemplated that,
[one should contemplate] the Ajapā mantra, which consists of the inhalation and exhalation of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu).
Having recited the *haṃsaḥ* mantra twenty-five times and offered it to the venerable Guru, (4).
Oṃ! O Goddess, whose girdle is the ocean and whose breasts are the circle of mountains!
O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch of your feet. (5)
O Goddess, the sustenance and nourishment of all beings always proceed from you.
By that truth, protect me, O Upholder; release me from evil.
O Goddess, he who performs worship with devotion without first performing his morning duties, [incurs a fault].
His worship is fruitless, like a ritual performed without purity.
Thus, having prayed to the Earth.

Following the dog's tracks, having placed his foot upon that [spot] and risen, while uttering the Astra-mantra over each step, he goes out from the house; having passed a distance of one throw of a *śakṭi* (sickle) toward the southwest or the southern direction outside the village, and having gone far, he performs the voiding of excrement and urine, as well as purification, sipping water (*ācamana*), and so forth.

Having performed the ritual according to the rules on days other than those prohibited, using the prescribed wood, one should cleanse the teeth with the mantra "klīṃ kāmadevāya sarvajana-priyāya namaḥ," scrape the tongue, rinse the tooth-stick, and place it before oneself.
Having abandoned [the body] in a pure place, having washed the face with the four Lakṣmī-vidyās to be described hereafter, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
one should extract [the consciousness] from the impure location by means of a stake consecrated with sesame, kuśa grass, flowers, scents, unbroken rice, and the weapon-mantra (astra).

Having taken earth, cow dung, and washed garments, one should go to a river or similar body of water; having cleansed the bank with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra* and having placed upon it *kuśa* grass and other items consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, one should perform the cleansing of the waist with water drawn from outside the bathing place, using fragrant substances such as *āmalaka* fruit for scrubbing and the removal of impurities.
Having performed the Vedic bath according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch using clay, cow dung, and other materials, and having stood in water reaching up to the navel; (4)

*Oṃ, beginning with "Today," etc.: For the sake of pleasing the glorious Supreme Deity, I shall perform the ritual bath according to the Tantric method.* Thus is the *saṃkalpa*. Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra, and having performed the placement of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth for the root mantra, as well as the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the hands, one should prepare a square bathing place (*tīrtha*) one cubit in size in front of oneself.
Having conceptualized. (4) ||
Oṃ, O Sun, the sacred fords within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays.
By that truth, O Lord of Gods, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford. (1)
Thus, having prayed to the Sūryātīrtha.
With the syllable *kroṃ* and the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*), having pierced the solar disk... (4)
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Sarasvatī!
O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in this water! (1)

Thus, having drawn the sacred water from the solar orb and having joined it with the previously prepared mandala of the sacred water before him by means of the root mantra, O Lord, [he should do so] again and again from the solar orb.
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hvāṃ hvīṃ hvūṃ hvaiṃ hvauṃ hvaḥ, O Tīrtha-śakti, who consists of universal bliss, come, come, svāhā!
Thus, having invoked the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha-śakti), one should meditate upon her in the center of that tīrtha-maṇḍala. As follows:

Consisting entirely of universal bliss, she destroys all sins without exception; she possesses the luster of the moon, has three eyes, and holds in her two upper hands a noose and a goad respectively.
With my two hands, I worship the Śrītīrtha-Śakti, who holds a golden pitcher filled with nectar and a choice rosary of pearls, accompanied by the twin rivers Gaṅgā and Sindhu. (1)

The visualization of the weapons is as follows: for the first two [deities], those situated above Dakṣa and so forth, the vessel is held by the two middle [hands]; for the other two, those situated below Dakṣa and so forth, it is held by the other [two hands].
Having meditated thus, one should worship her with that vidyā using the five services beginning with perfume, consisting of water. (4)

Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One! O Ambā, Ambālikā, Ambikā, Mahāmālinī! Come, come, O Blessed One, you who are the basin for all sacred bathing-places! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! O Gaṅgā, who are mounted upon the matted locks of Śiva; O Ambikā of the Gaṅgā! Svāhā!

Having consecrated [the water] seven times with this mantra, having stirred the water with the syllable *hrīṃ*, and having rendered it nectar with the *dhenu-mudrā* while pronouncing *vaṃ*, one should utter the first *kūṭa* of the root-vidyā and say: *ātma-tattvātmane namaḥ miḥ*.
Then, the second *kūṭa*: *vidyā-tattvātmane namaḥ*.
"Oṃ Tṛtīya-kūṭaṃ Śivatattvātmane Namaḥ.

Having thus projected the three principles (*tattva*) into the water, having visualized the *Śrīcakra* therein, and having invoked the Goddess from the lotus of the heart, one should perform the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*). Of those [goddesses]...
Having gratified the castes with the root-vidyā using the *yonimudrā*, one should consecrate that water eight times with mantras; then,

having submerged and emerged from that water three times while recollecting the deity and the mantra, one should sprinkle it three times on one's own head with the *kumbhamudrā* and the root-vidyā, perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), and satisfy the Goddess three times with the root-vidyā.

Having dismissed the Goddess, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) with the *tattvas* in the manner to be described; having come to the bank, put on two washed garments, and performed *ācamana* again, one should apply the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* with earth and other substances from the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and then apply the *tripuṇḍra* with sandalwood paste mixed with saffron. Having thus completed the Vedic *saṃdhyā*, one should perform the Tantric *saṃdhyā*.
One should perform it.
It is fourfold.
This is due to the divisions of morning, midday, evening, and midnight. Thus it is said in the Tripurārṇava:
The twilight prayer.
She should be known as fourfold: the infant, the maiden, and the young woman.
O Goddess, the twilight is proclaimed to be both mature and rootless. (1)
In the morning, the Great Goddess is considered to be Vidyāvāgīśvarī.
Kāmeśvarī at midday, and Tripurabhairavī at evening.
There, having sipped water according to the rules, bound his topknot with the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*), and likewise performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
he performed the ritual assignments (*nyāsa*) for the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, as well as the hand and six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) assignments, using the root mantra. Then,
having transformed the water into nectar with the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*) by means of his own *puṭa*, and having consecrated it eight times with the root mantra, [he used] that water.

Sprinkling one’s own head syllable by syllable with the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet, from *ka* to *kṣa*, accompanied by the nasal bindu (*m*), and sprinkling it three times with the root mantra; then, having meditated upon the Goddess in her described form within the solar orb, and having taken water in the right hand, [one recites]: *laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ*.
Having thus consecrated [the water] seven times with the mantras consisting of the five elements, and having consecrated it three times with the root-vidyā,

one should sprinkle one's own head three times with drops of that water using the left thumb and ring finger while reciting the root-vidyā; then, placing the remaining water in the left hand, one should [visualize] that water as being of the nature of light through the iḍā [channel].

Having drawn out all impurities situated within one's own body and washed them away, and having visualized that water— black in color— as flowing out through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī], one should again take that water in the right hand and, while meditating on a curved vajra-stone in one's left side, [recite] the *pāśupatāstra*: *oṃ ślīṃ paśu haṃ phaṭ*.
Having struck one's hands against that stone while reciting the mantra and having washed them,

one should take water in the right hand with the root-vidyā; then, visualizing it as having become one with the supreme nectar residing in the thousand-petaled lotus via the flowing channel (nāḍī), one should cause it to emerge through the opening of the eye from the cavity of the upper teeth.
Having placed that water in the left hand, one should sprinkle one's own head three times with that water using *kuśa* grass, while reciting the mantra: *amṛtāmāli svāhā*.
Having uttered the first peak-syllable: "I purify the principle of the self, svāhā. (4)
Having uttered the second peak-syllable: "I purify the principle of knowledge, svāhā. (4)
Having uttered the third peak-syllable: "I purify the Śiva-principle, svāhā!"
Having thus sipped water three times, and having again sipped water three times in the reverse order, as follows: (4)
Having uttered the third peak-syllable: "I purify the Śiva-tattva. (4)
The second peak-syllable is the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*); [I purify it] śo(0). The first peak-syllable is the principle of the self (*ātma-tattva*); [I purify it] śo(0). Again:
having uttered the entire mantra of knowledge, [one says] "I purify all principles, svāhā. Thus three times.
Thus, having sipped water nine times, one should perform the triple ācamana. (4)
Having worshipped three times with perfume, flowers, and unbroken rice grains while reciting the root mantra: "I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī."

Rising up without taking a handful of water, one should utter the first *kūṭa*: "O Vāgīśvarī, we meditate upon You"; uttering the second *kūṭa*: "O Kāmeśvarī, may You inspire our intellect"; and uttering the third *kūṭa*: "May that Śakti impel us."
To the venerable sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, this is the arghya offering; svāhā!
Having thus offered the *arghya* three times. (4)
Having worshipped the Sun three times with the mantra: "Hrāṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, I worship the glorious Sun; obeisance," (4).
Having offered three handfuls of *argha* water toward the sun with the mantra: "Hrāṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ, O Śrīsūrya, this is your *argha*, svāhā," (4).
Having offered libations three times to the Great Goddess with the root-vidyā, saying: "I offer libations to the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī; obeisance. (4)
Having offered libations three times with "Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Haṃ Saḥ, I satiate the illustrious Sūrya; obeisance," [one should proceed].

Having meditated upon the first *kūṭa* at the *mūlādhāra*, which possesses a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning, extending from the base up to the *brahmarandhra*; and having led that light through the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the *brahmarandhra*, one should invoke it into the orb of fire situated in space via the path of the nostrils.
One should meditate upon Vāgīśvarī, who has arisen from that splendor. It is as follows:
Yellow in complexion, clad in yellow garments, and adorned with yellow garlands, ornaments, and unguents.
She possesses the radiance of ten million flashes of lightning, and her youthful form is resplendent with a rosary of beads.
Seated upon a pedestal outside, she holds a book in her hand and wears yellow garments.
One should meditate upon her who is Vāgbhavī, born from the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], possessing three eyes, and smiling. (2)

Having thus meditated upon the fire-maṇḍala situated in space, (4) then, having uttered the *kūṭa*, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains three times, saying: "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Tripurā Vāgīśvarī. Then, having again uttered the *vāgbhava-gāyatrī* which is to be described hereafter, [one worships] Tripurā Vāgīśvarī.
Having offered three handfuls of water for the arghya with the mantra, "To the venerable sandals, I offer arghya; svāhā," he should cast them upward.

Again, having uttered the *prathama-kūṭa*, one should offer libations three times with the mantra: "I satisfy the venerable sandals of Tripurā Vāgīśvarī; obeisance. Then, bowing to the venerable Guru.

As before, having performed the breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the assignment of the seer and so forth (*ṛṣyādi*), and the six-limbed assignment (*kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), one should perform the following at the locations for the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*: the *praṇava*, the three *tārakas*, the root-mantra, and so on, up to the *nityā-vidyā* and *haṃsaḥ*.
Aṃ namaḥ. (3)

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* with these and other [mantras], and having recited the previously mentioned *turīya-gāyatrī* according to one's capacity, one should recite the *gāyatrī* of the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*. It is as follows:
Aiṃ! O Goddess Tripurā, may we know thee; O Mistress of Speech, may we meditate upon thee; may liberation impel us toward that end.
Thus one should recite the Vāgbhava-Gāyatrī according to one's capacity. Then, in the morning, one should recite the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) as follows: Namely:
There, in the morning, within the lotus situated at the mūlādhāra, in the circle of fire (vahnimaṇḍala), [one should meditate].
She is that eternal one whose form is the seed-syllable of speech, radiant like a mass of lightning. (1)
Her radiant hands hold a flower-arrow, a sugarcane-bow, a noose, and a goad.
She who assumes a form by her own will, whose nature is eternally imperishable throughout the ages. (2)
Then, with palms joined in reverence, they stood all around her, who was adorned with a water-clock and a veil.
She holds the knowledge-mudrā in her excellent hand and is devoted to the worship of Vāgbhava.
One should remember the nine lords in the root lotus within the yoni-maṇḍala.
The visualization of the weapons begins from the lower right hand and extends up to the upper right hand.
Thus, at each of the four junctions (saṃdhyā), having meditated in this manner.

[Beginning with] the Praṇava, the three Tārās, and the root-mantra, [recite] the Nityā-vidyā: *haṃ saḥ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛ ṝṃ hrīṃ*. I worship the Śrīpādukā of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, whose form is that of Śrī Prakāśānandanātha. (4)

Having uttered the root-vidyā as before, [one worships] the daily deity of the day: *haṃ saḥ ḷṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, "O you whose form is Vimarśānandanātha, I worship the venerable pādukā. (4)
Mūdiḥ vihaṃsaḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ;
[I worship] the sandals of Ānandānandanātha. (4)
Mūlaṃ dihaṃ saḥ caṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ. I worship the sandals of Śrījñānānandanātha-rūpa. Mūlaṃ dihaṃ saḥ ṭaṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ.
I worship the sandals of Śrīsatyānandanātha-rūpa. Mūlaṃ dihaṃ saḥ taṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ.
The sandals of Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha. (4)
The root-mantra here is: *paṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [the form] of Svabhāvānandanātha. || 4 ||
The root-mantra here is: Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the form of Pratibhānandanātha.
Mūṃ dīṃ haṃ saḥ ṣaṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, I worship the form of Subhagānandanātha.
Thus, one should recite the root-vidyā as being composed of the nine lords.
Then, having recited the Kālanityā-vidyā according to one's capacity on that day, [the rite is complete]. Thus ends the recitation of Kālanityā.
Then, meditating on the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) as possessing a radiance equal to a thousand rising suns, from the base [of the body] up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
and having recited the root-mantra one hundred and eight times, [one should visualize it] in the fire-maṇḍala situated in the external space.
Meditating upon the Mistress of Vāgbhava in the form previously described, one should recite the Vāgbhava-kūṭa one hundred and eight times in the morning.
Then, having performed three *prāṇāyāmas* and the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, as well as the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) upon the hands,

one should offer the completed recitation (*japa*) to the Goddess, prostrate, and praise her. Then, having dismissed the Root Goddess and Vāgbhaveśvarī from the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*) and the fire orb (*vahnimaṇḍala*) into one’s own heart and the *mūlādhāra*, [one should remember] the Guru.
"One should prostrate," it is said.
Thus concludes the procedure for the morning twilight devotion (saṃdhyā).
In this regard, meditation upon the Guru during the [appropriate] times for ritual action has been taught in the Rudrayāmala.
At the time of initiation, according to the specific form [of the disciple], in the rite of his own grace.
Having perceived him through that state of being, one should perform the daily ritual while meditating upon him.
The word "of the guru" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
This meditation on the Guru is to be understood as being superior to the morning recollection (*prātaḥsmaraṇa*) at times other than the morning.
O Īśānī, this morning twilight [rite] is always [required] for all ritual actions.
The minister must always strive for the accomplishment of counsel for the sake of prosperity. (1)
One who performs ritual acts while neglecting the morning twilight devotion falls into a lower state.
Having performed the morning twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), one should carry out the worship of the deity.
Impure, of very wicked conduct, he is excluded from all ritual actions. (3)
Having performed the morning twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), one should carry out the worship of the deity and other rites.
O Great Goddess, by performing [this] out of delusion, a man is born as a denizen of hell. (4)
O Śivā, having omitted the morning twilight devotion, as well as the fire-oblation or the water libation, [one incurs a fault].
A Brahmin who performs no [proper] cause and abandons [his duties] will certainly become a dog. (5)
O Goddess, even one who has mastered the Vedānta is born as a Piśāca.
Of all the twilight devotions as well, the morning twilight is the most important. (6)
Therefore, a Brahmin should not abandon her; by abandoning her, he would fall into hell.
Thus, according to the statement from the Tripurārṇava and other sources, this must certainly be performed; such is the teaching of Śiva.
Then, for the sake of a complete recitation (pārāyaṇa), one should perform sixty recitations during each hour (ghaṭikā).
And that consists of six recitations of the Mātṛkā over five days; likewise, it is stated there in the Rājapaṭala:
"Beginning from the rising of the Sun, one ghaṭikā [is assigned] in succession."
Each one of the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā [is repeated] through their permutations. (1)
It is said that her sixfold rotation occurs over five days.
Of that *mātṛkā*; this is the meaning.
Moreover, in each of the four ages, on the first day of that respective age, at the time of sunrise, the letter *A* arises.
Then, during the fifty *ghaṭikās* beginning with the second *ghaṭikā* and ending with the fiftieth *ghaṭikā*, the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*,
excluding the *visarga* and the vowels, arise at the time of their respective *ghaṭikā*-emergences.

Then, beginning from the fifty-first *ghaṭikā*, during the remaining ten *ghaṭikās*, the ten phonemes starting with *a* and ending with *ḷ* arise, each at the time of its own respective *ghaṭikā*-emergence.
Thus, on the second day, at the time of sunrise, the letter E arises.
Then, at the time of the rising of each respective hour (ghaṭikā), forty-nine letters beginning with *e* and twenty letters beginning with *a* arise. (2)
On the third day, at the time of sunrise, he caused [the sun] to rise.
Then, at the time of the rising of each respective hour (ghaṭikā), fifty-nine phonemes—from the letter *cha* to the letter *kṣa*, and from the letter *a* to the letter *ṇa*—arise. (3)
On the fourth day, at the time of sunrise, the letter *ta* arises.
Then, at the time of the rising of each respective *ghaṭikā*, fifty-nine phonemes—from the letter *ka* to the letter *kṣa*, and from the letter *a* to the letter *ma*—arise. (4)
On the fifth day, at the time of sunrise, the letter Ya arises.
Then, at the time of the rising of each respective ghaṭikā, forty-nine phonemes— ranging from the letter *ra* to *kṣa*, and from the letter *a* to *kṣa*— arise.
Thus, in five days, there occurs six recitations of the Mātṛkā.
In this manner, by means of these syllables in sequence, sixty recitations known as *pārāyaṇa* should be performed for each *ghaṭikā*.
Its specific manner is now demonstrated.

Then, there, the fifty letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, excluding the *visarga*, become ten groups of five; these are *aṃ, eṃ, caṃ, taṃ, yaṃ, tāṃ, māṃ, naiṃ, ṣaṃ, ṣṭhiṃ*. This recitation of sixty [syllables] should be performed; such is the procedure. (4)
The root is the daily *nityā* mantra: *haṃsaḥ aṃ*. (4)
The root is the daily Nityā-vidyā, *Aṃ Haṃsaḥ*.
Having thus repeated the fifty syllables ending with *kṣāṃ*, one should again repeat the group beginning with *ra*.
In this manner, there are sixty repetitions of the root mantra.
On the second day: (4) the root, the daily *nityā* mantra, and *haṃsaḥ*. Having likewise recited *aiṃ* and *evaṃ*, one should repeat the four groups (*varga*) thus recited;
then one should again repeat the first and second groups. In this manner, there are sixty repetitions.
On the third day, [one recites] the root[-mantra], the daily mantra, the Vidyā, and the Haṃsa;
thus, having repeated the three groups of consonants from *kṣāṃ* to *tr*, one should repeat the first three again.
In this manner, there are sixty repetitions of the root mantra.

On the fourth day (4), one should rotate the root-mantra, the daily mantra (*nityā-vidyā*) for that day, *haṃsaḥ*, and *yaṃ*. Having thus rotated the group ending in *kṣa*, one should again rotate the fifty letters beginning with *a* and ending in *kṣa*.

Thus, on the sixth day thereafter, one should again perform the recitation of the *pārāyaṇa* of the *ghaṭikās* incessantly, beginning once more with the letter *a* according to the method previously described.

Now, at this present time, practitioners should determine the elapsed days and so forth of the Kali Yuga according to the method stated in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) by means of the *ahargaṇa*, and then calculate up to the day of their own commencement.

Having determined the "rising syllable" (*udayākṣara*) by subtracting five from the elapsed days, one should know that on whichever day the rising syllable is the letter *ma*, the *ghaṭikā-pārāyaṇa* is prescribed to begin on that day; this recitation (*japa*) of the *ghaṭikā-pārāyaṇa* must be performed in the prescribed sequence at dawn alone.
According to the statement of the *Tantrarāja*, it should be performed during all three periods of time.
Now follows the midday twilight devotion.

Therein, having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth, as well as the libation to the Sun, in the same manner as the morning twilight rite, one should perform the seed-syllable twilight rite.
It is as follows:

There, at midday, meditating upon the red-colored Kāmarāja-kūṭa of the Mūlavidyā within the Anāhata-cakra, one should lead its radiance upward through the path of the Suṣumṇā, draw it out through the channel of the Nārā-puta, invoke it into the solar orb, and meditate upon the Goddess Kāmeśvarī who has become that very radiance.
It is as follows:
Red in color, richly adorned with garments and ornaments of deep red, she holds a noose, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and a boon-granting hand.
One should meditate upon Kāmeśvarī, who possesses a pure smile, is rich with the intoxication of youth, and has three eyes. (1)

Having meditated thus, (4) having uttered the *kāmarāja* syllable-cluster, and having worshipped three times with the mantra: "I worship the venerable *śrīpādukā* of the illustrious Tripurā Kāmeśvarī," (—) again (4) having uttered the *gāyatrī* of the *kāmarāja* syllable-cluster, [one says]: "I offer the *arghya* to the venerable *śrīpādukā* of the illustrious Tripurā Kāmeśvarī."

Having offered three handfuls of water with the *svāhā* mantra, one should again utter the *Kāmarāja-kūṭa* and satisfy [the deity] three times, saying: "I satisfy the venerable *Śrītripurākāmeśvarī-śrīpādukā*, obeisance."

Having preceded this with breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the like, and having performed the placement of the Mātṛkā as before, one should recite the Gāyatrī of the Fourth Vidyā as before, and then recite the Kāmarāja-kūṭa Gāyatrī.
It is as follows: *klīṃ*, we know the Goddess Tripurā; we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī; may that Klinnā inspire us.
Thus, having recited the Gāyatrī of the Kāmarāja-koṭa as many times as one is able, |||
One should recite the root-vidyā as being composed of the thirty-six principles.
It is as follows: then, there.
At midday, upon the solar disc at the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
The goddess, whose nature is the King of Desire, is as crimson as liquid lac. (1)
She is endowed with a flower-arrow, a bow of sugarcane, a noose, and a goad.
Surrounded on all sides by the thirty-six powers of the principles, with his own self as the foremost. (2)
She was surrounded by those adorned with red garlands, garments, ointments, and ornaments.
One should meditate on the enclosure of the ghaṭikās, which consists of the eternal syllables of the Yugas. (3)
They bear flower-arrows and sugarcane bows, and possess crimson bodies.
They dwell within the lotus of the heart, being solely devoted to the worship of Kāmarāja. (4)
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess.
(4) Having uttered the Root-Vidyā, the Daily Vidyā, and the word *haṃsa*, [one says]: *Aṃ śivatatvarūpiṇīṃ śrīmahātripurasundarīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. (16)
(4) Root-mantra: *Dinaṃ haṃ saḥ*. Kaṃ: I worship the sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, whose form is the principle (*tatva*) of Śakti. (16) Root-mantra: *Diṃ haṃ saḥ*. Khaṃ:
[I worship her] whose form is the principle of Sadāśiva. (16) Root-mantra: *Diṃ haṃ saḥ*. Gaṃ: [I worship her] whose form is the principle of Īśvara. (16) (4)

MŪ DĪ HAṂ SAḤ GHAṂ: She whose form is the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). MŪ DĪ ṄAṂ: She whose form is the principle of Illusion (*māyā*). MŪ DĪ HAṂ SAḤ CAṂ: She whose form is the principle of Limited Agency (*kalā*). MŪ DĪ HAṂ SAḤ CHAṂ: She whose form is the principle of Knowledge (*vidyā*). MŪ DĪ JAṂ: She whose form is the principle of Attachment (*rāga*).

(16) || (4) *Mū* *di* *haṃ* *saḥ* *jhaṃ*, she whose form is the principle (*tattva*) of Time (*kāla*). || (16) || (4) *Mū* *di* *haṃ* *saḥ* *ña*, she whose form is the principle of Necessity (*niyati*). || (16) || (4) *Mū* *di* *haṃ* *saḥ* *ṭaṃ*, she whose form is the principle of the Person (*puruṣa*). || (16) || (4) *Mū* *di* *haṃ* *saḥ* *ṭhaṃ*, she whose form is the principle of Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*). || (16) || (4) *Mū* *di* *haṃ* *saḥ* *ḍaṃ*.

I am she whose form is the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāra-tattva*). (16) (4) Mū, Di, Haṃ, Saḥ, Ḍhaṃ; I am she whose form is the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*). (16) (4) Mū, Di, Haṃ, Saḥ, Ṇaṃ; I am she whose form is the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*). (16) (4) Mū, Di, Haṃ, Saḥ, Taṃ; I am she whose form is the principle of hearing (*śrotra-tattva*). (16) (4) Mū, Di, Haṃ, Saḥ, Thaṃ; I am she whose form is the principle of touch (*tvak-tattva*). (16) (4)
MŪ~ HĀṂ SAḤ CAṂ: I am she whose form is the principle of the eye. MŪ~ HĀṂ SAḤ DHAṂ:
I am she whose form is the principle of the tongue. MŪ~ HĀṂ SAḤ NAṂ: I am she whose form is the principle of the nose.

(4) Mūṃ īṃ haṃ saḥ paṃ, she whose form is the principle of speech. (4) Mūṃ īṃ haṃ saḥ phaṃ, she whose form is the principle of the hands. (4) Mūṃ īṃ haṃ saḥ baṃ, she whose form is the principle of the feet. (4) Mūṃ īṃ haṃ saḥ bhaṃ, she whose form is the principle of the anus. (4) Mūṃ īṃ haṃ saḥ maṃ...

I am she who has the nature of the principle of sound (*śabdatattva*). I am she who has the nature of the principle of touch (*sparśatattva*). I am she who has the nature of the principle of form (*rūpatattva*). I am she who has the nature of the principle of taste (*rasatattva*). I am she who has the nature of the principle of smell (*gandhatattva*).
Di-haṃ-saḥ śaṃ, I am she whose form is the principle of fragrance. Di-haṃ-saḥ ṣaṃ, I am she whose form is the principle of space. Di-haṃ-saḥ saṃ, I am she whose form is the principle of wind.
Di-haṃ-saḥ haṃ, I am she whose form is the principle of fire. Di-haṃ-saḥ laṃ, I am she who is water.

*Tatvarūpiṇī* || (16) || (4) *Mū* (0) *di* (0) *haṃ saḥ kṣaṃ*, [I worship] the *pādukā* of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, who is the embodiment of the earth-tattva (*pṛthvī-tattva*). Thus, having recited the root-vidyā through the conjunction of the thirty-six *tattvas*, one should then recite the Kālanityā-vidyā one hundred and eight times, as before.

Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should contemplate the Kāmarāja-kūṭa within the heart-lotus— possessing the brilliance of ten million rising suns— as emitting rays of light that pervade from the heart up to the *brahmarandhra* and from the heart down to the *mūlādhāra*.
Meditating upon the *kadaṃbaka*, one should recite the *kāmarājakūṭa* one hundred and eight times.

Having offered the recitation preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the like, and having praised and prostrated to the Root Goddess and Kāmeśvarī, one should dismiss them into the heart as before. Thus ends the procedure for the midday twilight ritual (*madhyāhna-saṃdhyā-vidhi*).
Now follows the procedure for the evening twilight devotion (sāyaṃsaṃdhyā).
There, having performed the rites from breath control (prāṇāyāma) up to the satiation of the Sun as before, one should perform the seed-sandhyā (bījasaṃdhyā). It is as follows:

In the evening, having meditated upon the third *kūṭa* of the root-mantra— which resembles pure crystal— within the lunar orb at the *ājñā-cakra* in the *hakṣa*-lotus, extending as far as the full lunar orb situated in the *brahma-randhra*,
one should, through the flowing nostril, invoke it into the lunar orb located in space and [visualize] that which has arisen from it.
One should meditate upon the aged goddess. It is as follows:
White in complexion, adorned with white garments, unguents, garlands, and ornaments.
Wearing a mass of matted locks, her lotus-face shines with three eyes. (1)
And she had assumed a terrifying form, with her fangs slightly bared.
(2) She was covered with the graying hair of old age and possessed pendulous breasts.
Holding in her hands a noose, a goad, a book, and a rosary of crystal beads, she has arisen from the seed-syllable Śakti and stands within the orb of the full moon. (3)
One should meditate upon the primordial Supreme Śakti, who is served by those possessed of power.
The peaceful, infinite Amṛteśvarī, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (4)
The visualization of the weapons is as follows: the first [pair] is on the upper left and right, while the other [pairs] are on the lower left and right. Having thus meditated...

Having uttered the third *kūṭa* of the root-vidyā, saying "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Tripurāmṛteśvarī," and having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should utter the *gāyatrī* of the aforementioned third *kūṭa* and offer the *arghya* three times, saying: "I offer *arghya* to the *śrīpādukā* of Tripurāmṛteśvarī; svāhā!"
Again, having uttered the third peak-syllable: "I satiate the Śrī-pādukā of Tripurāmṛteśvarī; obeisance!"

Having thus satisfied [the deities] three times, and having performed the placement of the Mātṛkās preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites, one should recite the Gāyatrī of the Fourth Vidyā as before, and then recite the Śaktikūṭa-Gāyatrī.
It is as follows:

"OṂ SAUḤ! O Goddess Tripurā, may we know you; O Śākteśvarī, may we meditate upon you; may that Mṛtā inspire us. Having thus recited the Śakti-Gāyatrī twenty-eight times, one should recite the root-vidyā in the evening as consisting of the sixteen Nityās. It is as follows:
There,
in the evening, she [beheld] the lotus and the moon, which possessed a luster equal to the moon.
And [one should meditate on] Śakti, whose essence is the seed-syllable, and who is endowed with a bow, arrows, a noose, and a goad. (1)
The goddess who is eternal throughout the ages, the supreme Ghaṭikā, the Varaṇā.
Having visualized the Blessed Lady surrounded by her eternal retinues. (2)
Holding books and rosaries, they have smiling faces.
One should also remember the sixteen eternal ones during the evening time of the command. (3)
Thus the Goddess is to be meditated upon. (4)
The root mantra is the daily *nityā* vidyā: *(-) haṃsaḥ aṃ*. Having uttered the *kāmeśvarī nityā* vidyā:
*aṃ kāmeśvarī nityārūpiṇī śrīmahātripurasundarī śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*. (4) The root mantra is *di*: *haṃ saḥ āṃ*. Having uttered the *bhagamālinī* vidyā: *āṃ*.

Bhagamālinī, whose nature is eternal, Śrī (0). (16) (4) Having uttered the Mūla (0), Dina (0), Haṃ Saḥ Raṃ, and the Vidyā of Nityaklinnā: Iṃ, Nityaklinnā, whose nature is eternal, Śrī (0). Then, having offered the recitation preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), and having praised and bowed to the Goddess,

The ritual for the evening twilight.
Now follows the procedure for the fourth twilight devotion (turīya-saṃdhyā).
Then, at midnight, one should perform the fourth twilight devotion (*saṃdhyā*). It is as follows:

Having performed the meditation on the goddess within the orb of the sun, as well as the rites from breath control (prāṇāyāma) up to the ritual rinsing (ācamana) as previously described, one should meditate upon the fourth peak-syllable (turyakūṭa)— the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) consisting of thirteen syllables— possessing a luster like a ruby, within the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra-kamala), via the flowing nostril.
Having invoked her into the supreme space outside the circle of stars, one should meditate upon the Blessed Lady arising therefrom, possessing the form as previously described. (4)

Having recited the fourth peak-syllable (*turyakūṭa*) and worshipped three times with the mantra, "I worship the venerable *śrīpādukā* of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī," and meditating on her in her form as previously described, one should recite the fourth peak-syllable and offer the water of honor (*arghya*) three times with the mantra, "I present the *arghya* to the venerable *śrīpādukā* of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī; svāhā."

Having offered [the oblation] again, one should utter the fourth peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) and, having satiated [the deity] three times with the mantra "I satiate the venerable Mahātripurasundarī’s venerable sandals," and having performed *prāṇāyāma* and so forth,
one should recite the previously mentioned fourth *gāyatrī* according to one's capacity, as well as the *Kālanityā* mantra.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times and the seed-syllable of the third [tattva] one hundred and eight times,

and having offered the recitation preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites, one should praise the Goddess, dissolve her from the supreme space into the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus, and meditate upon oneself in the form of the *kāmakalā*.
The Procedure for the Fourth Twilight Ritual (Turīya-saṃdhyā-vidhi).
This fourfold twilight ritual is mandatory for those who worship this Vidyā.
When external power is available, the twilight worship at midnight, even in the form of meditation, should be performed.

If [the rite] is not performed on the second day, one becomes qualified to perform the ritual again after reciting the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) one hundred and eight times for the sake of expiation; such is the teaching of Śiva. Regarding the omission of bathing, twilight worship, and ritual adoration, the *Tantrarāja* states: "One hundred and eight [times]"; the remainder [of the sentence] is: "one should recite the root-mantra."

In this regard, [it is said]: "O Śambhu, the omission of the *saṃdhyā* must not be performed; for indeed, one who is initiated but devoid of the *saṃdhyā* does not enjoy the fruit of knowledge. According to this statement, the four *saṃdhyās* must necessarily be performed by practitioners (*sādhakas*); this is the summary. If, here, an omission of the *saṃdhyā* occurs through negligence...

It happens that at the time of another *saṃdhyā*, one should perform the ritual of the preceding *saṃdhyā* preceded by the prescribed expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and then perform the *saṃdhyā* for that specific time. And it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
One who has omitted the twilight prayer should perform the ritual of the preceding twilight prayer during the [current] twilight.
Having performed the concluding rite of the morning twilight devotion, one should perform [the subsequent rites] with a concentrated mind. (1)

Having thus performed the twilight rite (*saṃdhyā*) of Prakṛti, one should perform the triple libation (*trikatarpaṇa*), having completed the libations to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and enemies immediately after the morning twilight rite. Therein, preceded by the placement of the seers and other mantras (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*), one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and invoke the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) as before into the water in front of oneself with the mantra "oṃ āvāhayāmi."

Having rendered [the water] nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā* and consecrated it eight times with the root mantra, one should visualize the *śrīcakra* therein; then, having invoked the Goddess into its center preceded by the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) according to the method to be described, one should worship the Goddess in the water with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).

Having worshipped the deities of the limbs and the enclosures according to the procedure to be described, and having again worshipped the Goddess with the root mantra, one should recite the root-vidyā: "I offer libations to the venerable sandals of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī; obeisance."

Thus, having satiated the supreme nectar within the lotus-face of the Supreme Deity with the waters of that sacred ford— either one hundred and eight times, fifty-four times, or twenty-eight times according to one's capacity— one should worship the deities of the enclosure in their proper order, substituting the word "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) for the mantras prescribed in the ritual.

One should offer libations with a single handful of water for each [deity] while reciting "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*). If that is not possible, one should offer libations to the group of four beginning with Baṭuka, the six limbs, the three rows of young women (*yuvatī*), and the three lineages of gurus, together with the seventeen Nityās,
situated within the square, circle, and triangle mandala, along with their weapons and the triangular enclosure.
One should satisfy the Root Goddess, who is endowed with power.
If one is unable even for that, then having meditated upon the Goddess and worshipped Her in consecrated water, one should offer libations (tarpaṇa) to the Goddess alone;

such is the procedure for the libation rite (*tarpasāvidhi*). Then, having thus performed the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā-vandana*) and other rites, according to the method taught by one's own guru, [one should perform] twenty-seven hundred and thirty-six [repetitions].
One should perform the recitation (japa) of the Pārāyaṇa of the root-vidyā along with the thousandfold auxiliary vidyās arising from the syllables of the Yugas and the syllables of the Days.
The eternal vidyās pertaining to Kāla, as taught in the *Tantrarāja*, are now being extracted.
In that regard,

the thirty-six phonemes of the principles (tattva), beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣ', are each joined with the sixteen vowels of the sixteen Nityās, resulting in a total number of five hundred and sixty-four.
The phonemes are known as the "Full Mandala. These phonemes are the eternal time-vidyās;

of the previously mentioned number of vidyās, each single phoneme is the initial phoneme of thirty-six vidyās. Thus, all these phonemes are known as the Vāgbhava. [They correspond to] the previously mentioned thirty-six principles (tattvas).

The syllables of all these *vidyās*, joined with the letter *mā* (*ma*) through the process of *saṃdhi*, become the second syllables, known as the *Kāmarāja*. They are demonstrated as being accomplished solely through the recitation of the Pārāyaṇa.

Therein, first, the practitioner, having spread his seat in a secluded place—on the bank of a river or the like, or in a solitary spot, or in his own home—and having worshipped the seat with: "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Lotus-Seated One, the Power of the Foundation (Ādhāraśakti)," [should proceed].

The distinctions of the enumerations (paryāya-bheda) are fivefold; and so it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
From the day, from the weekday, from the fortnight, from the month, and from thirty-six days.
