Longevity, health, sovereignty, victory, and one's desired object, in due order.
They obtain [the fruits] through these graceful [practices], and thus one becomes possessed of the tradition. (2)
But on a single day, when the rotation occurs once, this is the rule.
One should begin at midday and conclude at midnight. (3)
And once, among the days of the week, on the first day, Sunday, during the recitation.
The first group belongs to Vaśinī, and the second to Kāmeśvarī. (4)
Having recited these two groups of mantras on Monday and the other five days as well, the practitioner of mantra—
During these joyful days, the wise practitioner should recite each [mantra] from the group one by one. (5)
And also during the fortnight, at one time, during the recitation, on the first lunar day and so forth.
One should recite daily the vidyās arising from these two rows. (6)
On the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth lunar days, respectively.
When the vessels are full, the wise man should mutter the vidyās belonging to the four rows. (7)
Day by day throughout the month, the wise man should indeed contemplate one single womb.
One should recite the six mantras arising from the full moon and the two wombs in their proper sequence while dreaming. (8)
In this manner, during thirty-six days, one should indeed enter each single womb.
The wise one should recite this every day; in this way, they become perfected. (9)
No science whatsoever exists in the worlds that is equal to these.
Therefore, by means of these methods, one should accomplish everything desired. (10)
Whatever is desired by oneself, that very thing becomes difficult to do yet easy to do.
Remaining steadfast, one should satisfy [the deity] through recitation, libations, fire-offerings, worship, and sprinkling. (11)
Having recited the vidyā fifty times, endowed with devotion, [one attains the fruit].
One is released from shackles, from hardships, and from most terrible enmities and conflicts. (12)
Having repeated it one hundred times, various powers of knowledge arise.
Even a woman who has been barren obtains sons endowed with all excellent qualities. (13)
Having repeated the Vidyā one hundred and fifty times with devotion, facing the east.
He diligently seeks a wife endowed with virtues, beauty, and other such qualities. (14)
By repeating this [mantra], a maiden shall obtain a husband endowed with all virtues.
She obtains sons, grandsons, and so forth, and she prospers, endowed with wealth. (15)
By reciting them two hundred times, one will certainly be liberated from poverty.
One who possesses three hundred [gold pieces] is endowed with the sixth stage, and one who possesses four hundred is wealthy. (16)
With five hundred [lines] one becomes a chief minister (bhūpa), and with six hundred, a king (nṛpa).
But with seven hundred [servants], Ramā did not leave his lineage. (17)
With eight hundred of them, all kings are his servants.
Thus, with nine hundred [arrows], he struck the women of Kandarpa’s forest. (18)
Having thus recited it nine hundred times, one shall obtain all desires.
The worship of them all together is said to bestow the accomplishment of all aims. (19)

Thus [ends the section]. Now follows the explanation of the difficult points (*viṣamapadavyākhyā*) among these: from "dinataḥ" up to "bhavet," consisting of two and a half verses, is clear in meaning. In one cycle of recitation, by means of the *Kālanityā* Vidyās numbering twenty thousand seven hundred and thirty-six—

The meaning is that when the recitation (*japa*) of the *sahamūla-vidyā* is performed daily according to the prescribed rule for that specific number; and on the days of the week, beginning from Sunday and ending with Saturday, while these [days] are observed, we shall clarify the groups (*varga*) of the *Vaśinī* goddesses and others in the upcoming section on ritual placement (*nyāsa*). A "group" (*varga*), "row" (*paṅkti*), and "womb" (*yoni*) are synonymous.

This is the section on the ritual procedure (*paryāya*). The *sekha* (initiation), the *abhiṣeka* (consecration), and the steadfast, unwavering devotee have been explained through verses beginning with "fifty" and so forth.

The recitation for specific desires (*kāmya-japa*) pertains exclusively to the *Kālanityā* Vidyās. Furthermore, although there are many other ritual applications for fulfilling desires (*kāmya-prayoga*), we have not written them here for fear of making the book too voluminous.
They are not to be understood merely from the teacher or from the scriptures.
Now follows the method for constructing the Kālacakra.
Then: first, having made a dot (bindu) somewhere, one should draw a circle around it with a measurement of six finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
outside of that, likewise at intervals of one finger-breadth each, sixteen circles should be produced, so that together with the first circle, seventeen circles are completed.

Having divided the squares by thirty-six lines so as to produce thirty-six paths consisting of sixteen cells each, one should write [the vowels] in the path at the front of the *sukha* (starting from the outermost cell) by moving inward: *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ*. Then...
In the second row reached by proceeding clockwise, starting likewise from the outermost square, [the syllables are]:
ka kā ki kī ku kū kṛ kṝ kḷ kḹ ke kai ko kau kaṃ kaḥ. In the third row:
kha khā khi khī khu khū khṛ khṝ khḷ khḹ khe khai kho khau khaṃ khāḥ ||
In the fourth row: ga gā gi gī gu gū gṛ gṝ gḷ gḹ ge gai go gau gaṃ gaḥ.

In the fifth row: gha, ghā, ghi, ghī, ghu, ghū, ghṛ, ghṝ, ghḷ, ghḹ, ghe, ghai, ghaṃ, ghaḥ. In the sixth row: ṅa, ṅā, ṅi, ṅī, ṅu, ṅū, ṅṛ, ṅṝ, ṅḷ, ṅḹ, ṅe, ṅai, ṅo, ṅau, ṅaṃ, ṅaḥ. In the seventh row: the *ca*-group (*cavarga*). Thus, one should place [the letters] in every row everywhere.
The *cha*-group is in the eighth path; the *ja*-group is in the ninth path; the *jha*-group is in the tenth path; the *ña*-group is in the eleventh path; and the *ṭa*-group is in the twelfth path.

(13) The *v* group. (14) The *ḍ* group in the path. (15) The *ḍh* group in the path. (16) The *ṇ* group in the path. (17) The *t* group in the path. (18) The *th* group in the path. (19) The *d* group in the path. (20) The *dh* group in the path. (21) The *n* group in the path. (22)

In the *vīthī*, the *p*-group. (23) In the *vīthī*, the *ph*-group. (24) In the *vīthī*, the *b*-group. (25) The *bh*-group. (26) The *m*-group. (27) In the *vīthī*, the *y*-group. (28) In the *vīthī*, the *r*-group. (29) In the *vīthī*, the *l*-group. (30) The *v*-group. (31) In the *vīthī*, the *ś*-group. (32) In the *vīthī*, the *ṣ*-group.

(33) In the [outer] path is the *savarga* group; (34) in the path is the *havarga* group; (35) in the path is the *lavarga* group; (36) in the path is the *kṣavarga* group. Having thus inscribed the letters of the full mandala, numbering five hundred and seventy-six, within the thirty-six paths, one should [inscribe them] in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Ā.
Having written the four syllables "ī haṃ saḥ," one should produce three circles outside the outermost circle,
draw an eight-petaled lotus with filaments, and construct a square on the outside;
in this arrangement of syllables, all the letters should be positioned so that they face the deity situated in the center.
They should be written down.
Thus is the method for the arrangement of Kālacakra.
There are five hundred and seventy-six divisions of this wheel; all of that— the method of worshipping the Goddess therein and its fruits—
should be understood from the Guru and from the scriptures, for fear of excessive prolixity in this book.

It has not been written here for fear [of prolixity]. Having thus performed the recitation (*japa*) of the *Pārāyaṇa*, the preceptor (*guru*), after bowing to the guardians of the directions and the planets, takes a vessel filled with pure water; remembering his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) in his heart, chanting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) or a hymn (*stotra*), remaining silent and fixing his gaze only upon his own feet, he returns to his own home.

Standing at the door, recollecting one's own sins—whether known or unknown—and uttering the *praṇava* (Oṃ): "My mind, which was previously divine, has become possessed by sin; expel that sin from my mind!
Phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ! Salutations to you, O Sun, Moon, Yama, Time, and the five great elements!"
These are the nine witnesses here in this world of auspicious and inauspicious karma. (2)

Having recited thus, and looking toward both sides, upward, and in the middle with a wrathful gaze while uttering "HŪṂ PHAṬ," one should become well-disposed, enter the interior of the house, wash the hands and feet,
perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and [draw] with vermilion or other pigments upon a level patch of ground in the courtyard smeared with cow dung.

Having spread one's own seat within the prepared and cleansed mandala, (4) and having worshipped the seat with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti)," one should sit there facing east and [meditate upon] Mārtaṇḍabhairava as described below.
Having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the mantra, [one should say]: "Salutation to the divine portion in the head for the *ṛṣi*."

In the mouth: (4) Salutation to the goddess Gāyatrī, the metre. In the heart: (4) Salutation to the deity Śrīmārttaṇḍabhairava. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should say with palms joined in reverence: "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the offering of the *arghya* to the Sun, for the attainment of all my desired goals."

Then: Oṃ ghrāṃ hyāṃ dhrāṃ, salutation to the heart. Oṃ dhrīṃ hyrīṃ dhrīṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ dhruṃ hyrūṃ dhruṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ dhraiṃ hyraiṃ dhvaiṃ, hūṃ to the armor. Oṃ dhrauṃ hyrauṃ dhrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. Oṃ dhraḥ hyraḥ.

*Dhraḥ astrāya phaṭ.* Having thus performed the assignment of the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) on the two hands from the thumbs to the little fingers, one should also assign them to the heart and other parts of the body. Then follows the meditation (*dhyāna*).
In his beautiful hand-lotuses, he holds a discus, a spear, a noose, a goad, a radiant rosary, and a skull— each possessing its own natural luster resembling gold, a lotus, and coral.

We worship him who holds lotus-like hands, who is beautiful with three eyes and the four faces of the Vedas shining forth, who is the Sun-god seated upon his beloved, wearing a jeweled crown and radiant with necklaces. (1)

The first [pair] is for the upper two [hands] starting from Dakṣa; the second is for the lower two starting from that same [Dakṣa]; the third is for the lower two starting from that same [Dakṣa]; the fourth is for the other two lower [hands] starting from that same [Dakṣa].
Such is the meditation on the weapons. Having thus meditated upon [the deity] as one with oneself and having worshipped mentally, [one proceeds].

Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp, filaments, and a circle within a triangle using vermilion, saffron, and so forth in a vessel made of copper or other materials; and having drawn a circle outside that, followed by a square provided with four doors, one should then trace three circles around it— thus having prepared the worship mandala.

There, having offered a flower with the Sūrya-mantra and having prepared the general arghya (sāmānyārghya) according to the procedure to be described, one should sprinkle the mandala, oneself, and the ritual implements with that same water after it has been consecrated twelve times with that mantra.

Therein: Oṃ Maṃ, salutation to Maṇḍūka. Likewise, salutation to Kālāgnirudra; salutation to Mūlaprakṛti; salutation to Ādhāraśakti; salutation to Kūrma; salutation to Ananta; salutation to Varāha; salutation to Pṛthivī; salutation to Kṣīrasamudra; salutation to Śvetadvīpa; salutation to Kalpavāṭikā; salutation to Maṇimaṇḍapa.

Having worshipped in successive layers with "Homage to the Jewel Balustrade" and "Homage to the Jewel Lion Throne," [one worships] in the square in the four directions starting from the east and in the center: "Oṃ Praṃ, Homage to Prabhūta"; [Homage to] Vimala; [Homage to] Sāra; [Homage to] Samārādhya; and in the center, [Homage to] Paramasukha. Then, in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya):
Oṃ dhaṃ to Dharma, to Jñāna, to Vairāgya, and to Aiśvarya; then, in the four directions starting from the front [of the deity]: Oṃ aṃ to Adharma, namaḥ.
To Ignorance, to Non-detachment, to Non-mastery, to the Center, to Ananta, to Padma, to the Root-stalk of Bliss, to the Fiber of Consciousness,
to the Petals consisting of Prakṛti, to the Filaments consisting of the Transformations, and to that which is enriched by the fifty seed-syllables of the phonemes.

Salutation to the pericarp, which is the form of all principles (*sarvatattva*). To *saṃ* (for *sattva*), *raṃ* (for *rajas*), *taṃ* (for *tamas*), *āṃ* (for the *ātman*), *aṃ* (for the *antarātman*), and *paṃ* (for the *paramātman*).
Hrīṃ to the Self of Knowledge; (-) Maṃ to the Fire Mandala; (-) Uṃ to the Moon Mandala; (-) Aṃ to the Sun Mandala.
Then, upon the eight petals and in the center: Rāṃ to Dīptā; (-) Rīṃ to Sūkṣmā; (-) Rū to Jayā; (-) Reṃ to Bhadrā; (-) Raiṃ to Vibhūti; (-) Roṃ to Vimalā; (-) Rauṃ...

To Amoghā—*raṃ*; to Vidyutā—in the center, *raḥ*; to Sarvatomukhī—[in the four directions]. Having thus worshipped the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭhaśakti*), [one should worship] the pedestal with: "Oṃ, salutation to the Yoga-pedestal consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, belonging to the Sun.
Having thus worshipped the pedestal, [one should worship] in its pericarp, in the four directions starting from the east: "Oṃ Uṃ, salutation to Uṣā."

Having worshipped the four powers with "Oṃ praṃ Prajñāyai," "Oṃ praṃ Prabhaiyai," and "Oṃ saṃ Saṃdhyāyai," one should recite the Mārtaṇḍabhairava mantra and, saying "I fashion the form of Śrī Mārtaṇḍabhairava," mentally project the form in the center; then, having again recited the mantra—
Having worshipped the form with "Salutation to the Form of Mārttaṇḍabhairava," and taking a handful of flowers with both hands,
one should meditate on the Lord in the form of light within the heart-lotus and [invite Him] through the path of the *suṣumṇā* into the nostril.
Having brought that splendor through the path of the *puṭa* [tubes] into the handful of flowers held in the hand, one should recite the Sūrya mantra:

"O Lord Sūrya, come, come here! By casting the handful of flowers upon that image, one should invoke that splendor into the [hand-held] handful of flowers and meditate upon the deity in the form as previously described.

Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the previously mentioned six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), having performed the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and having displayed the lotus and discus gestures (*mudrā*), one should recite the Sūrya mantra: "O Śrīmārtaṇḍabhairava, this is your seat;
obeisance (*namaḥ*). Likewise: "This is your water for honor (*arghya*); *svāhā*," [offering it] upon the head; "This is your water for the feet (*pādya*); obeisance," [offering it] at the feet.

"This is for you, the water for sipping (ācamanīya); it is *sudhā* (nectar)—[place it] in the mouth. "This is for you, the honey-mixture (madhuparka); it is *sudhā*—[place it] in the mouth. "This is for you, the water for sipping; it is *sudhā*—[place it] in the mouth. In the same way, [offer] the bath (*snāna*); "obeisance" (*namaḥ*). "The water for sipping; it is *sudhā*—[place it] in the mouth. "A garment (*vāsas*); obeisance. "The water for sipping; it is *sudhā*—[place it] in the mouth. "A sacred thread (*upavīta*); obeisance. "The water for sipping; it is *sudhā*..."
In the mouth: "Obeisance to the ornament; obeisance to the fragrance; obeisance to the flowers, vauṣaṭ.
Having thus offered the services ending with the flowers, one should then perform the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇa-pūjā). It is as follows:
In the pericarp, in the four directions starting from the east: Oṃ hyraṃ sūryāya namaḥ; Oṃ hyrī bhāskarāya namaḥ; Oṃ hyraṃ bhānave namaḥ; Oṃ hyreṃ ravaye namaḥ.

Then, in the four directions beginning with the southeast (āgneya), having worshipped the five forms (*pañcamūrti*) with: "Oṃ hyrauṃ, obeisance to Divākara," [one worships] upon the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus: in the southeast, "Oṃ dhrāṃ hyrāṃ dhrāṃ, obeisance to the Heart"; in the southwest, "Oṃ dhrīṃ hyrīṃ dhrīṃ, obeisance to the Head"; in the northwest, "Oṃ dhruṃ..."

*Hyrūṃ dhrūṃ*, salutation to the *śikhā* (crest-lock) in the northeast (*īśānya*). *Oṃ dhrai hyraiṃ dhraiṃ*, salutation to the *kavaca* (armor) in the four directions starting from the east. *Oṃ dhraḥ hyraḥ dhraḥ*, salutation to the *astra* (weapon) in front of the deity. *Oṃ dhrau hyrauṃ dhrauṃ*, salutation to the three eyes. Then, on the eight petals:

Beginning from the foremost petal of the deities: Oṃ soṃ, homage to Soma; Oṃ maṃ, homage to Maṅgala; Oṃ buṃ, homage to Budha; Oṃ bṛṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati; Oṃ śuṃ, homage to Śukra; Oṃ śaṃ, homage to Śanaiścara; Oṃ rāṃ, homage to Rāhu; Oṃ keṃ, homage to Ketu.

Outside of that, one should then worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and their weapons: Oṃ Laṃ, obeisance to Indra. In the same way: Raṃ, obeisance to Agni; Ṭa, obeisance to Yama; Kṣaṃ, obeisance to Nairṛti; Vaṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa;
Yaṃ, obeisance to Vāyu; Saṃ, obeisance to Soma; Haṃ, obeisance to Īśāna.

Between Indra and Īśāna (–), and between Nirṛti and Varuṇa (ca): *Āṃ* to Brahmā; *Hrīṃ* to Ananta (0). Then, on the sides of the guardians of the directions (0): *Vaṃ* to the thunderbolt (*vajra*) na (0);

*Śaṃ* to the spear (*śakti*) (–); *Daṃ* to the staff (*daṇḍa*) na (0); *Khaṃ* to the sword (*khaḍga*) (0); *Pāṃ* to the noose (*pāśa*) (0); *Aṃ* to the goad (*aṅkuśa*) na (0); *Gaṃ* to the mace (*gadā*).

Having worshipped the enclosures in this manner— saying "Salutation to the triple trident," "Salutation to the five lotuses," and "Salutation to the discus"— and having offered incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth,
one should fashion a circular mandala before oneself and [say]: "Salutation to the mandala for the arghya of Mārttaṇḍabhairava."

Having thus worshipped the mandala, one should place a vessel made of copper or another suitable material— capable of holding one *prastha* of water and washed with the *astra-mantra*— together with its support (*ādhāra*) therein. Meditating upon it as the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) and reciting the solar mantra, one should fill it with pure water.
Having placed kusha grass, sesame seeds, śyāmāka grain, saffron, sandalwood, gorochana, and karavīra flowers [into the vessel],

and having covered it with kusha grass, one should recite the mantra of the Sun— *dhriṃ hyrau dhriṃ*— one hundred and eight times while touching the vessel; then, one should meditate upon Mārtaṇḍabhairava.
Having touched the ground with both knees and lifted that vessel with both hands up to his head, [he recites]:

*Dhṛṃ hrīṃ dhṛṃ. To the illustrious Mārtaṇḍabhairava, accompanied by the Śakti Prakāśā, whose self consists of the twelve *kalās*, who is surrounded by the planets, zodiac signs, lunar mansions, lunar days, weekdays, *yogas*, and *karaṇas*, and who is seated upon a lotus.*

Having offered the *arghya* with the mantra "I offer the *arghya* to the glorious Sūrya, svāhā," and having covered his own field of vision with the *mahāmudrā*, while visualizing Ārttaṇḍabhairava as being completely drenched by the nectar of that *arghya*, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the previously mentioned Sūrya-mantra.

Having recited the mantra preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other practices according to one's capacity, and having offered the recitation preceded by breath control and other practices, and having praised and prostrated,
saying "Forgive me," one should dismiss Mārtaṇḍabhairava into the sky with the mantra: "Obeisance to Tejaścaṇḍa in the northeast."
One should discard the floral remains.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the offering of water to the Sun.
This is the primary ritual procedure.

In the event of inability to do that, one should offer the *arghya* according to the prescribed rite while meditating upon Mārtaṇḍabhairava together with his retinue within the solar orb in the sky; this is the middling procedure (*madhyama-kalpa*). The inferior procedure (*adhama-kalpa*) consists of offering the *arghya* by means of the mantra alone. Thus is the *sūryārghya* prior to the worship.
Giving is necessary.

Then, having performed the worship of Śiva, one should perform the worship of the pavilion door. In this regard, since it is said that "the earthen [liṅga] bestows all accomplishments," the worship of the earthen liṅga (pārthivaliṅga) is highly recommended. As for the method of its worship:
on a clean spot smeared with cow dung, having first worshipped one's own seat according to the procedure prescribed for the worship of the Sun, one should proceed.
There, having sat facing north and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) beginning with "Today... and ending with the recording of the lunar date, saying:
"For the sake of the qualification for the worship of the venerable Supreme Deity, I shall perform the worship of the earthen liṅga.
Thus having resolved.
Oṃ, O Goddess who supports all foundations, this clay, which is of your very form—
"I shall accept you with a clear mind; O Suprabhā, become the purpose for the Liṅga. (1)
Having thus requested the ground— *oṃ harāya namaḥ*— and having taken pure, bright, and very smooth earth from a clean spot— having purified it with *oṃ maheśvarāya namaḥ*—
this is the joining (*saṃghaṭṭana*).

Having prepared [the seat] in front of oneself and having seated [the deity] upon the pedestal and so forth with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the Trident-bearer (Śūlapāṇi)," one should take a handful of flowers, meditate on the God in the form of light within the heart, draw that light out through the path of the nostrils, and, having joined that light to the handful of flowers held in the hand, [recite]: "Oṃ, O Wielder of the Pināka bow, come here..."

Having invoked [the deity] into that *liṅga* by scattering an *añjali* of flowers while reciting "Come, come," and having established [the deity] with "O Trident-bearer! Stay here, stay here," one should bathe [the deity] with pure water while reciting "Obeisance to Paśupati," and offer perfumes and flowers while reciting "Obeisance to Śiva. Then, beginning from the front of the altar and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction (*pradakṣiṇa*) around the altar, [one should perform the rites] while reciting "Oṃ..."

Salutation to Śarva, whose form is the earth; Oṃ, salutation to Bhava, whose form is water; Oṃ, salutation to Rudra, whose form is fire; Oṃ, salutation to Ugra, whose form is wind; Oṃ, salutation to Bhīma, whose form is space; Oṃ, salutation to Paśupati, whose form is the sacrificer.

Oṃ, salutations to Mahādeva, whose form is the Moon. Oṃ, salutations to Īśāna, whose form is the Sun. Having worshipped thus, one should worship [the goddess] in the conduit with: Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutations to Umā. Then, having worshipped three times with: Salutations to Śrī Śiva, together with his limbs and his retinue, one should say: Oṃ, salutations to Śiva.
Thus, having offered those services beginning with incense and ending with betel three times.
Oṃ, to the one great soul whose sole purpose is the bestowing of the wisdom of omniscience.
Salutations to you, O God, Lord of gods, who are devoted to the welfare of all beings. (1)
Endowed with infinite fame, he is seated upon many thrones.
O Supreme Lord, endowed with infinite splendor, salutations be unto You! (2)

O Lord of the Universe, who transcends the high, the low, and that which is beyond both; you who are the cause of the arising and subsistence of all things, and the means for accomplishing every purpose—homage be to you! (3)
Inherently pure, you are enjoyment that destroys all diseases;
O Yogi, Great Yogi, Lord of Yoga, homage be to you! (4)
Having performed the consecration of the Liṅga, one should recite this hymn of praise.
The man who always hears this highly meritorious hymn to the Liṅga, (5)
He is not reborn in saṃsāra and attains the eternal state.
Therefore, with every effort, one should listen to the hymn of praise to the Liṅga. (6)
Freed from the cloak of evil, one attains the supreme state.
Having thus offered praise, one should recite the mantra with a one-pointed mind.
O Maheśvara, [one who is] deficient in limbs, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in the prescribed procedure.
"O Lord, you have been honored by me; therefore, forgive what was done through negligence. (1)
Even though [they are] corrupted, discarded, and defiled by [wrong] conceptions;
And with hair and insects cast away, you have been worshipped by me, O Lord. (2)
O Lord, [this occurs] when one's mind is attached elsewhere or when one is devoid of ritual action.
Though worshipped with impurity of mind, speech, and body, O Three-eyed One! (3)
And whatever arghya and other offerings were made by me with a defiled vessel;
And not out of a tamasic disposition; therefore, forgive me for this, O Lord. (4)
With a mantra lacking syllables, and with a flower that is fruitless.
O Mahādeva, you have been worshipped; may all of that be forgiven by me. (5)
May my vow reach completion, and may its fruit be inexhaustible for me.

Within the four oceans of nectar, each extending for ten million yojanas, there is a most wonderful island made of the nine precious gems, measuring ten million yojanas in width and length, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns; in its center, at one-third of its extent, is the place named Madanonmādana, filled with various flowering creepers and kadamba trees.

In the center of that third portion is the Nandana garden; it shines like ten million suns, is encircled by a blazing golden wall, and is adorned with various fragrant halls, arches, and gateways embellished with diverse jewels.
It is filled on all sides by hosts of gods, such as Indra and others, who have arrived for the sake of service, and it is composed of rubies.

On the other five parvan days—namely, the teacher’s birthday, the day he attained knowledge, one’s own birthday, the new moon (darśa), and the day of the teacher’s death—one should perform [the rite]. Regarding the full moon (pūrṇā), he states a special rule: "Or else," meaning that if a day endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics cannot be found, then on the full moon itself, during the auspicious rising of one's own breath.

He states another alternative: "Or, at all times, there is the auspicious rising. In this regard, for one who has realized the Self through the knowledge of reality (tattvavid), having disregarded everything such as the lunar days and weekdays as proclaimed [by others], the meaning is that for his own breath, there is only the auspicious rising. This position—that "one should act"—applies to those who have attained perfection (siddha); it is not to be practiced by others.
"One who has attained perfection should perform the consecration, not one who is proud of his knowledge," because it is stated in that very same [text].

"The Goddess is to be worshipped by the best of men according to the prescribed rite. And so it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
Or, respectively, in a gem, gold, silver, copper, or stone.
Having fashioned the mandala of the wheel, one should establish it and also worship it.
For the attainment of fortune, fame, sons, wealth, health, and so forth, [one should worship] the beloved of Lakṣmī.
Upon the stone slab of the Dṛṣadgaṇḍikā mountain.

This is because of the statement in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*: "On stones from the Gaṇḍakī river, and on gold, silver, and copper. Now, he states the specific number of times for worship according to the particular metal, as recorded in the *Ratnasāgara*:
O beloved, for as long as one lives, [the practice] should be performed with gold; with silver, twenty-two years;
with copper, twelve years; and with birch bark, half of that.
Thus, in the *Sārasaṃgraha*.
In copper it lasts for twelve years, but in crystal and other such materials it lasts forever.
Among those, however, the crystal one shall be the bestower of all accomplishments.
The word "Śrīcakra" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Now, he states the specific fruit resulting from a specific location: in the *Lakṣasāgara*:
Drawn upon the ground with vermilion powder, it grants all desires.
This golden yantra brings prosperity to the entire royal lineage.
A yantra fashioned from silver, when worn upon the body, bestows health and fulfills all desires.
A yantra fashioned from copper is considered to bestow all forms of sovereignty.
For this yantra, O Goddess, when inscribed on crystal, bestows whatever the mind desires.
This yantra, engraved upon ruby, bestows both sovereignty and liberation.
A yantra fashioned from gomedaka is considered to bestow all forms of sovereignty.
This machine fashioned from emeralds is the destroyer of all enemies.
A yantra produced from the three metals is considered to grant all accomplishments.
The Goddess said:
O Maheśvara, how should the yantra produced from the three metals be fashioned?
Tell me that out of compassion, if I am dear to you.
The illustrious Lord said:
There were ten portions of gold and sixteen of silver.
One should fashion a beautiful pedestal from copper using one-twelfth part [of the total weight].
Upon that pedestal, one should cause the construction of the Śrīcakra.
It is declared to bestow peace, to grant nourishment, and to destroy all enemies.
It is considered to be the producer of longevity and health, the bestower of luster, and the giver of nourishment.
Now, regarding that very [subject], there is a threefold division of the cakra according to its method of expansion (prastāra).
Listen to the threefold nature of the wheel: that which is spread upon the earth, that which is above, and that which has Mount Meru as its center.
O Goddess, for those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla), the arrangement consists of downward-pointing lines.
O Maheśānī, for those dwelling in the mortal world, there is an upward-pointing line.
Among those dwelling in the heavenly world, the king of machines is known as Meru.
O Maheśvarī, beginning from the Bhūpura and ending with the Bindu.
I have described everything as being progressively elevated in the form of Mount Meru.
A group of nine lines with equal upper and lower lines is proclaimed as the "upper-line" (ūrdhvarekha) type.
From the conjunction of the lower lines, the expansion of the earth has been described by me.
The true nature of the King of Yantras has been revealed to you by me out of affection.
O blessed lady, you must keep this secret at all times, as if it were your own private secret.
Now, the fruits of these three types of *prastāras* and another *prastāra* are described in the *Tantrarāja*.
Beginning from the square, one proceeds in sequence through the nine wheels.
From the highest point to the lowest, the center should be a wheel; it is both destruction and wealth.
By rising through the three triads, one attains that state of non-birth and the glory of Śrī.
An elevation occurring in the sequence of one, two, or three [steps] conduces to prosperity and fame.
Nine identical forms for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
Likewise, in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
O Goddess, there is gradual elevation, then the acquisition of wealth, and thereafter death.
The earth-wheel should have sixteen spokes, and it should also be equal with eight spokes.
O Īśānī, the remainder, when increased, becomes the attainment of wealth and the bestower of progeny.
O Goddess, it is a square, level, with sixteen spokes and so forth, ending with the bindu.
O Goddess, mutual elevation leads to prosperity and fame.
Beginning from a square, it should be marked with a dot and straight lines.
In the same way, prosperity, fame, and health conduce to immortality. Thus it is said.
Now, he describes the prohibited metals and other prohibited substrates for the Śrīcakra.
In the *Tantrarāja*:
Furthermore, in the case of lead, brass, and so forth, the opposite of what was previously stated occurs.
One should never place it upon a wooden plank, a cloth, or a wall.
If it was established through delusion, greed, or even ignorance;
It utterly uproots one's lineage, wealth, and offspring in every respect.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Lakṣasāgara*:
It should never be made with tin, lead, or iron.
He states the measurement of the seat of the Śrīcakra and the quantity of the materials.
In the *Kulamūlāvatāra*.
The fire-altar is one finger-breadth in width, extending from east to west and from south to north.
The beautiful pedestal for the image should be made measuring one pala.
One should fashion a square measuring half a barleycorn on all sides.
And upon that pedestal, one should cause the construction of the Śrīcakra.
In the Sautrāmaṇi Tantra.
A straight line brings prosperity; a curved line brings poverty.
"Agni should be one finger-breadth in width and half a barley-corn in height. Thus it is said.
In the ocean of a hundred thousand [verses].
The measurement for gold and likewise for silver is one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
The same number as previously stated for copper applies to the maṇida according to one's desire.
"Agni is one finger-breadth wide" and "of gold" are stated because it is divine; the meaning is that it is three finger-breadths in width and length.

A *pala* is measured as three hundred and twenty *guñjās*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), specific gems such as *puṣpanīla* and others are denoted. Furthermore, the width of three finger-breadths (*tryaṅgula*) is according to the measurement of a standard finger (*mānāṅgula*).

Furthermore, the construction of altars, pedestals, palanquins, chariots, and so forth, must be performed using only the *mānāntarāṅgula* (the finger-breadth of the measurement system) and not by any other; this is according to the statement in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*.

Since the substratum of the Śrīcakra is denoted by the word *pīṭha*, the statements establishing the meaning of the word *pīṭha* have already been written above. Furthermore, the definition of the *mānāntara-aṅgula* (the finger-breadth based on the measurement of the deity) is found in the Kapila Pañcarātra itself.
The intermediate finger-measure (mānāntarāṅgula) is defined by eight barley-corns placed crosswise.
Or, the interval between measures shall be three rice grains placed in a straight line.
Now follows the method for this consecration.
In that regard, it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
First with honey, ghee, and milk, and then with coconut water.
Then, one should consecrate [the patient] with water boiled with medicinal herbs containing the letters *akṣara*.
Having invoked [the deity] at the auspicious moment and worshipped it, one should establish it upon the wheel and perform worship.
The attainment of the eternal reality arises from time; these [deities] are to be worshipped in sequence by means of the Vidyā.
One should recite the mantra while touching it with the tips of the fingers, and one may also worship the Śrīcakra.
Having performed this for three days, one should thereafter practice the daily ritual sequence.
With perfumes, flowers, fresh incense, lamps, food offerings, and libations.
For three nights, one should worship the Goddess together with the practitioners of yoga.
Thus, in the case of the installation of a goddess, this is the sequence that brings about her presence.
Now follows the ritual application of this.
In that regard, the wheel fashioned according to the aforementioned measurement— if it is made of a metal such as gold and the like— is cleansed with sour liquid,
purified according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas, and its fire-consecration (*agnyuttāraṇa*) performed; having placed it in some vessel,
one should [perform the rites] during an auspicious month, fortnight, and asterism as will be described in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā*).
On a day distinguished by an auspicious lunar date (tithi), weekday (vāra), astrological division (karaṇa), and hour (muhūrta), and favorable for the practitioner with respect to the moon and stars,
having consecrated [the image] individually with honey, clarified butter, milk, coconut water, and fragrant water during a fixed zodiacal sign (sthiralagna),
one should again consecrate it with the decoction water of fifty-syllable medicinal herbs.
Having washed [the image] with fragrant waters as before, and having performed the worship of the door and so forth up to the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha),
one should place that cakra upon that pedestal; then, having worshipped it in the same manner up to the mantra of the pedestal,
one should invoke the Goddess into that cakra by means of the daily Vidyā of that day and the third syllable (kūṭa) of the Vighnāntaka mantra.

Having worshipped each [deity] three times with the root-vidyā, and having performed the worship of the limbs and the surrounding deities (aṅgāvaraṇa-pūjā) according to the prescribed rule, one should again consecrate the cakra by touching it while reciting the Kālanityā-vidyās twenty-one thousand six hundred and thirty-six times, as previously stated.

Having worshipped according to the sequence of the Śrīcakra-pūjā, and having likewise worshipped and gratified the Goddess and the initiates (sāmayikas) with incense, lamps, and various kinds of food offerings, one should bow and dismiss them. One should not dismiss the Goddess for three days. Every day, at the three junctions of the day, one should perform the sequential worship. Thus it is said.

Once the *cakra* has been installed, one should perform the daily worship and other rites. This same procedure should be understood to apply even for the installation of an image (*mūrti*). The distinction there is that in the case of a permanent [image], there is no ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). Having thus raised up the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*), one should offer the *bali* to all beings in front of oneself to the left, according to the procedure to be described, and then the *bali*...
To the north of that place, one should meditate upon the King of Birds, as follows:
The root-wing is Aṣṭāpada, the king is Vajrāṅkura, and the peak of the golden wing is Hāṭaka.
Accepting the ruby as its golden crest-jewel, its lotus-face shone with the brilliance of its beak. (1)
Shining with the splendor of the sun, fire, and the moon, and adorned with rubies that illuminate his three eyes.

His entire mass of body hair glows with the luster of blue sapphire stones; his head is radiant with a crescent moon; and he is beautiful with a necklace formed by the drops of the Gaṅgā falling in succession from his head, which is covered by the waves of that river as it flows over the mass of his excellent, tawny matted locks tied in a double-knot above the sun.

It is beautiful with garlands shimmering from a pair of serpents arising from his arms—their hoods joined in a sequence that crushes the elephants of the quarters, their five-fingered tips knotted together, and their tails bound in a knot at the base. (3)
Indeed, the Vaiśya women, bound by their girdles, with the playful brilliance of the moon upon their shimmering pair of feet,
and agitating the quarters of the world with the swelling of their bells, have brought the lineage of the lord of the land to a state where he is the sole protector against the hosts of enemies.

With its noose-like form, it causes the destruction of the multitude of trembling bulls; it is terrifying with the flashing hissing of the lord of serpents' coils, and it endures everything for a moment as the mass of hoof-strikes falls upon it. (4)
[He saw him] in the form of a bird, devouring the multitude of enemies of his devotees.
With a one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon the locust, the Sālva, and the form. (5)
Thus, having meditated upon Śiva in the form of a locust: (4) Oṃ ai hrī śrīṃ oṃ namo bhagavate śalabha sālvāya pakṣirājāya mama śatrūn nāśaya nāśaya ghe ghe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī Śalabharudra. Having meditated upon the goddess Śalabhī, who resembles a locust, on the left side of the locust [deity]: (4) Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, O Śalabhī, O Śālvi, O Queen of Birds!
Destroy, destroy my enemies! Ghe ghe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Śrī Śalabhī Devī.

Having worshipped the Śalabha and the couple with the mantra "I worship the auspicious sandals (śrīpādukā)," [one should worship] in the eastern direction of the Cakra [the deity] who has the brilliance of the sun at the end of the aeon, filling the entire three worlds with his splendor,
red-eyed, with tawny hair, the cause of fear to the enemy clan, possessing terrible fangs and a loud laugh.
I meditate in my mind upon the primordial Lord known as Cakrin, the enemy of Mura, who bears in his own arms the discus, conch, mace, lotus, a very broad club, bow, noose, and goad.

The visualization of the weapons is as follows: the first [weapon] is on the upper right and left of Dakṣa; the second is on the lower right and left of that same [Dakṣa]; the third is on the lower right and left of that [second weapon]; and the fourth is on the lower right and left of that [third weapon]. Having thus meditated upon the Śrīsudarśana:
(4) Oṃ sahasrāra hūṃ phaṭ, homage to the glorious Sudarśana. Having thus performed the worship:
To the south of that [is] Aghora,
who resembles a water-laden cloud, possessing terrible fangs, three eyes, and holding a serpent, and who is clad in red garments and smeared with red unguents.
I meditate upon him bearing an axe, a hand-drum, a sword, a staff, an arrow, a bow, a trident, and a human skull. (1)

The meditation on the upper [faces] begins with *dakṣa* and so forth; for those situated below the first [face], there is another beginning with that same [name]; for those situated below the second, there is yet another; and for those situated below the third, there is the rest—such is the meditation on the upper faces. Having thus meditated upon Rudra in the form of Aghora: (4) *hrīṃ sphura (2) prasphura (2) ghoraghorattaratanurūpa caṭa (2) pracaṭa (2)*.
Kaha (2) vama (2) bandha (2) ghātaya (2) hūṃ phaṭ, obeisance to Aghora Rudra.
Having thus fully worshipped Aghora Rudra, [one proceeds] to the west.
Seated in the center of a golden lotus, three-eyed and resembling a flash of lightning,
she holds a conch, a discus, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, while bearing a digit of the moon.

One should meditate upon her who dwells in the Vindhyas, who wears necklaces, armlets, strings of pearls, and earrings; who is praised by Indra and the other gods; who has a moon-like face; and who has a lion standing at her side. (1)
The visualization of the weapons begins from the upper left hand and ends with the lower left hand.

Thus, having meditated upon the illustrious Durgā: (4) "Arise, O Puruṣī! Why do you sleep? Fear has come upon me. Whether it be possible or impossible, O Blessed One, pacify that for me, svāhā! At this point, at the time when it is about to be recited, one should remember the vidyās.

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Śrī Durgā," (4) having placed the materials for worship, such as sandalwood paste and flowers, on one's right side, (4) while recollecting the mantra "Hāṃ Hīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ," one should gaze at the flowers and other items with the *ārāc* mudrā and the divine vision (*divyadṛṣṭi*), [and look at] the vessel filled with water situated on the left side.

Having touched the water-pot with the left hand while reciting "Āṃ," (4) having touched the water within the pot with the tip of the right hand while reciting "Chrauṃ," (4) one should touch the flame of the lamp while reciting "Raṃ.
Then, having washed the hands, [one should place] "Aiṃ Guṃ" and "Obeisance to the Gurus" on the left, (4) and "Gaṃ" and "Obeisance to Gaṇapati" on the right. (4)
First, having prostrated with palms joined (*añjali*) saying "Obeisance to the Illustrious Supreme Deity," and having placed the *saṃghaṭa* mudrā upon his head, [he recites]:
*hasrauṃ hasakṣamalavayarāṃ haṃsakṣamalavayarūṃ hasakṣamalavayarīṃ haisrāṃ hasakṣamalavayarūṃ śrīparapāvaka sarvārādhya*.
O Lord of all cities, O Universal Preceptor, O Self-Preceptor, Śrī Gurunātha! Rahasakṣamalavayarūṃ Hasrauṃ Haṃsa Kṣamalavayarīṃ Hasakṣamalavayarūṃ Hasakṣamalavayarāṃ Śrī Śambhu!

Having placed the Śrī Guru-pādukā upon one’s own head with the mantra: *Guru hasrauṃ (48) Śrī Amukānandanātha Amukī Devyambā Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and having worshipped it again with this very same Vidyā using sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, and flowers, one should display the five mudrās beginning with sandalwood paste and say: "Obeisance! (namostu).

Having prostrated with the *namaskāra-mudrā* while reciting "To the Guru," etc., one should perfume both hands by rubbing fragrant substances with the *karaśuddhi-vidyā*: *aṃ āṃ sauḥ*. Then, taking fragrant flowers with the mantra *hasraiṃ*, one should crush them with the left hand, purify them with *rauṃ*, and smell them.
Oṃ hauḥ! May all those who harm me, the assailants, go to destruction.
May death, disease, fear, and afflictions fall upon the heads of our enemies!
Having recited this, one should cast that flower far toward the northern direction with the *nārāca* mudrā.
Then again, having purified the hands by rubbing them against one another with the *karaśuddhi* mantra, [one should assign the syllables]:
(4) *aṃ namaḥ* to the two middle fingers; (4) *āṃ namaḥ* to the two ring fingers; (4) *sauḥ namaḥ* to the two little fingers;
(4) *aṃ namaḥ* to the two thumbs; (4) *āṃ namaḥ* to the two index fingers; and [the same] to the palms and backs of the hands.

(4) Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) with "sauḥ namaḥ," and having performed the triple pervasive placement (*trivyāpaka-vinyāsa*) from the head down to the feet with the mantra "aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ namas tripurasundari māṃ rakṣa rakṣa," one should again utter this [mantra] and perform three upward claps (*tāla*) with the sounds produced by the index finger and thumb, ten times.

Having formed a boundary for the directions by rotating three times around one's own head with the two hands in the shape of crossed tridents, thereby creating three external enclosures, and having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, one should effect the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi) through twelve repetitions of the Praṇava.

One should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). It is as follows: one should contemplate from the feet to the knees the locus of earth—square, marked with a vajra, yellow in color, having Brahmā as its deity, presided over by the *nivṛtti* kalā, and joined with the seed-syllable *laṃ*. From the knees to the navel is that of water...

Having meditated upon the *sthāna* (location) as being shaped like a half-moon, white in color, marked with lotuses on both its two peaks, presided over by Viṣṇu, established in the *kalā* of *Pratiṣṭhā*, and joined with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*;
and [having meditated upon] the fire-maṇḍala from the navel to the throat as being triangular in shape and endowed with a *svastika*.
Having meditated upon [the element] as red in color, presided over by Rudra, associated with the Vidyā-tattva and the Kalā-tattva, joined with the seed-syllable *Raṃ*,
one should visualize the wind-maṇḍala from the throat up to the space between the eyebrows as being hexagonal in shape, marked with six dots, and surrounded by a circle.
One should visualize [the element] as black in color, having Īśvara as its presiding deity, presided over by the power of Peace (Śānti-kalā), and joined with the seed-syllable *Yaṃ*.
It extends from the space between the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmaraṃdhra*), is located in the sphere of space, is circular in shape,
marked by a banner, smoke-colored, has Sadāśiva as its presiding deity, and belongs to the state Beyond Peace (*śāntyatīta*).
Having meditated upon [the syllable] *haṃ*, presided over by *kalā* and joined with the seed-syllable.

Therein, within the body composed of the five elements, one should visualize the lotus of one's own heart— arisen from the bulb of dharma, possessing a stalk of knowledge, endowed with eight petals of the eightfold powers, and having supreme detachment as its pericarp— and within that pericarp, the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which is the size of the tip of an awl.

Having meditated upon the supreme consciousness (paracid-rūpa), which is as radiant as the flame of a lamp yet veiled by beginningless impurities, one should form the *yoni-mudrā* and, according to the previously described method, raise the Kuṇḍalinī from the *mūlādhāra*. Following the path of the *suṣumṇā*, [one proceeds] from the *mūlādhāra* through the *anāhata* and other centers (*cakra*) situated along the way, [engaging with] the phonemes (*varṇa*) and the presiding deities (*varṇādhipa*).

Meditating on the individual soul (jīvātman) as being swallowed by the stream of the supreme deity brought into the heart-lotus, one leads that stream— consisting of the letters and their presiding deities located in the wheels beginning with Viśuddhi—
along the path of the Suṣumṇā to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), where it rests within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus.

Having joined the individual soul (*jīvātman*)— which resides in the midst [of the body] as the aggregate of all the presiding deities of the phonemes (*varṇādhidevatā*) within the light of the Supreme Self— with the mantra "haṃsaḥ," and having performed protection with the *astra* [mantra],
one should effect the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) by leading Kuṇḍalinī back to her own place. It is as follows:

There, at the location of the earth, having recollected the foot-faculty, the act of going, the destination, the smelling of odors, the earth, Brahmā, the Nivṛtti-kalā, and the Samāna-vāyu, [one should recite]: *oṃ hrāṃ brahmaṇe pṛthivyadhipataye nivṛttikalātmane hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

With this mantra, one should withdraw all of them through the door of Kuṇḍalinī into the midst of the waters. Then, in the place of the waters, having meditated upon the hands, the tongue that tastes the rasa to be given, the water, Viṣṇu, the Pratiṣṭhā, and Udāna—(4) *oṃ hrīṃ viṣṇave jalādhipataye pratiṣṭhā-kalātmane hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus.

By means of the mantra, one should dissolve all of those into the fire-principle (*vahni-tattva*) through the gateway of Kuṇḍalinī. Then, having recollected the anus, the emission, the *visarjanīya* sound, the eye, the fire, Rudra, Vidyā, and Vyāna in the place of fire, [one should recite]: (4) *oṃ hrūṃ rudrāya tejodhipataye vidyā-kalātmane hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus, by this mantra—

One should dissolve all of those into the wind-maṇḍala. Then, having recollected the worship at the station of wind—its object being touch, the tangible, and the Lord of Wind (Vāyvīśvara), along with the peaceful offerings—one should [recite] the mantra: *Oṃ hraiṃ īśvarāya vāyvadhipataye śāntikalātmane hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus, by this mantra.

One should withdraw all of those into the space-element (*ākāśa*). Then, having recollected the vital breaths—speech, the face, the organ of speech, the sound to be uttered, the ear, the space, Sadāśiva, and Śāntyatītā—within the space-element, one should recite: (4) *oṃ hrauṃ sadāśivāyākāśādhipataye śāṃtyatīta-kalātmane hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus.

Having withdrawn all those [elements] into the Kuṇḍalin by means of the mantra, one should withdraw the Bindu-śakti into the Nāda-śakti, and the Nāda-śakti into the Para-śakti by means of the Praṇava: (4) Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Thus, having united that supreme power (*paraśakti*) with the previously mentioned Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and having contemplated the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*)— earth and the others— in their respective order as becoming one with the supreme reality (*paratattva*), one should contemplate the Person of Sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) within the left side of the solitary body. It is as follows:
In the left side of the belly stands the personification of evil, with the luster of lampblack;
he has the murder of a Brahmin for his head and shoulders, and the theft of gold for his two arms.
The drinking of liquor is associated with the heart, and violating the teacher's bed with the two hips.
Association with them is a pair of steps that brings sin upon every limb and member of the body.
With body hair bristling from minor transgressions and red beard and eyes.
One should visualize him as wrathful, bearing a sword and shield, with a wicked person within his belly.

Having thus meditated upon the personification of sin, one should, at evening, by reciting the seed-syllable thirty-two times while drawing in the breath through the left nostril, join it with the wind residing in the navel within a six-cornered wind-mandala; there, one should meditate on the black-colored wind-seed syllable *Yam*.
While performing the *kumbhaka* (retention), one should repeat the seed-syllable *yaṃ* sixty-four times;
then, together with the great wind arising from it, having completely dried up the personification of sin within one's own body,
one should repeat that wind-seed-syllable sixteen times and exhale that wind through the right nostril.
By means of the seed-syllable *raṃ* (32), having drawn in the breath through the right nostril by means of inhalation (*āvartana*) and joined it with the *mūlādhāra*,

one should contemplate the red-colored fire-seed *raṃ* within the circle of fire situated there; then, by means of retention (*kuṃbhaka*), while repeating the seed-syllable *raṃ* sixty-four times, [one should meditate] upon the great fire arising from that.

Having burned his own body along with the personification of sin, and having repeatedly recited the fire-bīja "raṃ" together with the ashes of that personification of sin, he should exhale that air through the left nostril.
Again, through the left nostril (32), having filled [the body] with air together with the seed-syllable *vaṃ* and joined it at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
one should contemplate there the white-colored nectar-seed-syllable *vam* within the lunar orb of consciousness.
By means of retention (*kuṃbhaka*) (64), while revolving the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, [one should sprinkle] one's own body with the stream of nectar issuing from it.

Having sprinkled ashes while reciting the seed-syllable *vaṃ* sixteen times, one should exhale that air through the right nostril (*vīrecya*). Then, filling the air again through the right nostril while reciting the seed-syllable *laṃ* thirty-two times,
one should join it with the earthly mandala situated at the *mūlādhāra*, [visualizing] "therein [is] blood" (*tatra raktam iti*).
Having meditated upon the earth-seed syllable *laṃ* as yellow in color, while reciting that *laṃ* seed-syllable sixteen times during the retention (*kuṃbhaka*) of breath,

one should expel that air through the left nostril by means of the fire arising from it, which has condensed the ashes produced by the nectar-drenched [air]. Then, while reciting the *laṃ* seed-syllable sixteen times, one should exhale that air through the left nostril.

Again, through the left nostril, having filled the breath along with the syllable *hrīṃ* (32), one should contemplate the *māyābīja*— the color of the rising sun— throbbing within the drop (*bindu*) situated at the *mūlādhāra*. While retaining the breath (*kuṃbhaka*),
one should rotate the *māyābīja* (64) and thereby [reconstruct] one's own body, complete with its limbs such as hands and feet.

Having visualized the perfected seed-syllable of illusion (māyābīja), one should exhale that wind through the right nostril while not causing it to revolve; thus, having produced the gross body, one should produce the subtle body. It is as follows:

Therein, from the Supreme Self (Paramātman) situated within the previously mentioned thousand-petaled lotus, one brings forth the Supreme Power (Paraśakti), who is the embodiment of the Will of the Supreme Brahman manifested as the desire to create the entire universe— reciting "Oṃ Hrīṃ Namaḥ"— and leads her from the presence of the Supreme Self to her own station; thereafter, the Power of Sound (Nāda-śakti), and then the Power of the Bindu (Bindu-śakti).

Having created the *bindu* by means of the *praṇava*, and having extracted from the presence of Śakra the *kuṇḍalinī*—which is the cause of the creation of the entire universe—by means of the *praṇava*, one should then [recite]: "Oṃ hraum! Salutation to Sadāśiva, the Lord of Space, whose self is the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta-kalā*). [This concerns] the vital breath, the state beyond peace, Sadāśiva, space, the sense of hearing, and sound.

One should place the speech that expresses what is to be said in the location of space (*ākāśa*). Then, from the sphere of space (*ākāśamaṇḍala*), one should perform the pacification of the downward breath (*apāna-śānti*) with the mantra: *Oṃ hrāṃ īśvarāya vāyvadhipataye śāntikalātmane namaḥ*. This is the touch of the Lord (*īśvara*) upon the wind, which is the object of touch.

One should place the objects of that [sight], bliss, the anus, and the wind in the location of the anus. Then, with the mantra: (4) *oṃ hrūṃ rudrāya tejodhipataye vidyākalātmane namaḥ*, one should place Vyāna, Vidyā, Rudra, Tejas, the eyes, form, the visarjanīya, the visarga, and the anus in the location of fire. Then, (4) *oṃ*...

With the mantra "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of waters, whose self is the *kalā* of *pratiṣṭhā*," one should establish the hands of Viṣṇu— whose *udāna* is *pratiṣṭhā*, whose tongue is water, and who bestows the essence of taste— in the place of the waters.

Then, with the mantra: *Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the earth, whose essence is the Nivṛtti-kalā*, one should establish the Samāna breath, the Nivṛtti-tattva, Brahmā, the earth, the sense of smell, the object of smell, the action of going, and the organ of the feet in their respective places within the earth-element. Then, having established Kuṇḍalinī in her own place by means of the Praṇava (*Oṃ*), [one should proceed].
Having meditated upon the pervasion of the powers of Nāda, Bindu, and Parā within one's own body by means of the Praṇava,

[one should contemplate] the individual soul (jīvātman), together with the withdrawn phonemes and their presiding deities, being drawn up from the Supreme Self residing in the Brahma-randhra through the Kuṇḍalinī into the Ājñā and other cakras.

Establishing the presiding deities of each respective phoneme, and having brought [them] into the heart-lotus by means of the mantra "so'ham," one should establish the individual soul (jīvātman) in the heart-lotus; then, via the path of the *suṣumṇā*,
while establishing the presiding deities of each respective phoneme in the *maṇipūraka* and other wheels (*cakras*), [one should descend] to the *mūlādhāra*.

Having led [the element] there, one should establish it. Then, having visualized one's own body as being free from all impurities, consisting of radiant energy (*tejas*), and fit for the worship of the deity—this is the purification of the elements (*bhūti-śuddhi*).
Having performed the purification of the elements as prescribed, one should proceed with the ritual of worship.
Likewise, worship performed without devotion shall yield a contrary result.

One should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths). It is as follows: On the head: (4) *Oṃ namo brahmaviṣṇuśivebhya ṛṣibhyaḥ*. In the mouth: (4) *Oṃ namo ṛgyajuḥsāmabhyaśchaṃdobhyaḥ*. In the heart: (4) *Oṃ namo devatāyai parāprāṇaśaktyai*. In the secret place: (4) *Oṃ āṃ namo bījāya*. In the feet: (4) *Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ śaktaye*.

*Namaḥ*. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "At the navel: *kroṃ*, salutation to the Kīlaka," one should speak with palms joined in reverence: "This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of the consecration of my vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). (4) *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ a kaṃ (4)* [to the five elements], to the Self consisting of ether, air, fire, water, and earth: *āṃ*, salutation to the heart. (4) *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ iṃ caṃ (4)*... [and so forth].
Oṃ śabdasparśarūparasagandhātmane ī śirase svāhā. (4) Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ uṃ ṭaṃ (4) śrotratvakcakṣurjihvāghrāṇātmane ūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ.

(4) Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ eṃ taṃ (4) to the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ; aiṃ to the armor, huṃ. (4) Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ oṃ paṃ (4) to the self of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure; oṃ to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ. (4) Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ aṃ yaṃ (9) to the mind, intellect, and ego.

Having performed the nyāsa of the mantras "Cittittātmane aḥ" and "Astrāya phaṭ" from the thumb to the little finger, and having likewise performed these on the six limbs beginning with the heart; then, from the navel to the two feet: *Āṃ* *Namaḥ*; from the heart to the navel: *Hrīṃ* *Namaḥ*; from the head to the heart: *Kroṃ*.

Homage! Then, in the center of the heart-lotus: (4) *yaṃ*—homage to the self of the skin. On the eastern petal: (4) *raṃ*—homage to the self of blood. On the western petal: (4) *laṃ*—homage to the self of flesh. On the southeastern petal: (4) *vaṃ*—homage to the self of fat. On the northwestern petal: (4) *śaṃ*—homage to the self of bone. On the northeastern petal: (4) *ṣaṃ*.

*Mañ* to the Self of the Marrow; salutation! On the petal of Nairṛti: *Saṃ* to the Self of Semen; salutation! On the northern petal: *Haṃ* to the Self of Vital Breath (*prāṇa*); salutation! On the southern petal: *Laṃ* to the Self of Life-force (*jīva*); salutation! Again, on the pericarp: *Kṣaṃ* to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); salutation! Thus one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*). Then follows the meditation (*dhyāna*).
Seated upon a red lotus on a red ocean, she holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows.
I bow to the Goddess, who is red in color, possesses three eyes, and holds a trident and a skull in her lotus-like hands. (1)

Having meditated thus, placing the hand upon the heart: (4) *oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ haṃ saḥ sohaṃ mama prāṇā iha prāṇāḥ* (4) *oṃ āṃ* (14) *mama jīva iha sthitaḥ* (4) *oṃ āṃ* (14) *mama sarvendriyāṇi* (4) *oṃ āṃ* (14) *mama...*

"Speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and breath—having come here, may they remain happily for a long time, Svāhā! Having thus recited the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra three times, one should meditate upon one's own body as consisting of light. This is the procedure for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). One should recite the mantra "Oṃ" sixteen times while placing the hand on the heart.
By Śrī Vidyānandanātha, the beloved son of Śiva and Umā.
Thus, in the Ocean of the Jewels of Good Fortune, the third wave has passed. (1)
[Thus ends the third wave in the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*, composed by Śrī Śrīvidyānandanātha, a resident at the pair of lotus-feet of the venerable Saccidānandanātha. (3)
Now follows the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
And here, within this Vidyā, it is fourfold due to the distinctions of the Śuddhaka, Kalāmūrti, and Prapañcayāga.
In this Vidyā, there are also thirteen types beginning with the pure (śuddha): the pure; joined with the bindu; joined with the visarga;

joined with both bindu and visarga; preceded by hṛllekhā; preceded by Lakṣmī; preceded by the Kāma-bīja; preceded by Māyā-Śrī; preceded by the Kāma-bīja; encapsulated by Bālā; and encapsulated by Parā.
The Śrīvidyānvita is of two kinds: the Haṃsa and so forth, and the Paramahaṃsa and so forth. Even when endowed with Kalās, it is likewise twofold.

The placement (nyāsa) consists of the digit of the Tāroksa [the syllable Om], the digit arising from the triad of splendors, and the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. The Mūrti-nyāsa is also twofold, distinguished as Keśavādi and Śrīkaṇṭhādi. The fourth is the Prapañcayāga.

Therein, first, having performed three rounds of *prāṇāyāma* with the letters of the *mātṛkā*, one should begin the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Among these, inhalation (*pūraka*) is performed with the vowels, retention (*kuṃbhaka*) with the five groups of consonants, and exhalation (*recaka*) with the letters beginning with *ya*. This is the *mātṛkā-prāṇāyāma*. Having thus performed the three rounds of *prāṇāyāma*, one should perform the *nyāsa*; therein, next—
First is the placement of the pure Mātṛkās.

Oṃ. Of this Śrī-Śuddha-mātṛkā-nyāsa, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), the venerable Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā), the consonants are the seeds (bījāni), the vowels are the powers (śaktayaḥ), and the Unmanifest (avyakta) is the pin (kīlaka).
Its application (viniyoga) is in the nyāsa as an auxiliary to my Śrīvidyā. Having thus joined the palms in reverence and recollected the seer and the other [limbs], [one should proceed].

One should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) on the head and other parts as follows: On the head: (4) *namaḥ* to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*). In the mouth: (4) *namaḥ* to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*).
In the heart: (4) *namaḥ* to the goddess Śrīmātṛkā-Sarasvatī. In the secret place: (4) *namaḥ* to the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the consonants (*hal*).

*Namaḥ*. [Place] *namaḥ* at the two feet (4). *Namaḥ* to the Vowels (*svarāḥ*) and the Śaktis at the navel (4). *Namaḥ* to the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) Kīlaka. Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), one should say with palms joined in reverence, pervading all limbs: "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the ritual placement as a limb of Śrīvidyā. Then, on the palm of the right hand: *a namaḥ*; on its back: *ā namaḥ*; on the fingers of the right hand... [and so on].

I bow. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the ten vowels beginning with *ī* and ending with *ū* upon one’s own ten fingers, starting from the right thumb and ending at the left thumb, one should place the vowels beginning with *au* and ending with the *visarga* on the left palm, its back, and its surface. This is the *saṃhāra-nyāsa*. [Then] starting from the right palm...

One should place the vowels ending with the *visarga* on the left palm; this is the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*. Having placed the eight vowels beginning with *ḷ*, along with the *bindu* and *visarga*, starting from the left little finger and ending at the [left] palm, one should then place the eight vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *ṛ*, along with the *bindu*, starting from the right palm and ending at the [right] little finger.

"One should perform the placement (nyāsa) joined with the *visarga*; this is the procedure for the placement of the stationary [vowels]. Thus, having performed the placement of the Mātṛkā vowels, one should place the letters beginning with *ta* up to *śa* (the "peaceful" consonants) in fifteen locations, starting from the base of the left little finger and ending at the tip of its thumb; then, starting from the right thumb...

Having placed the letters from *ka* to *ṇa* at the tips of the little fingers, one should simultaneously place the five groups of letters from *ṣa* to *kṣa* as pervasive [mantras] on both hands, starting from the thumbs and ending with the little fingers.
Thus, having performed the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) with the letters of the Mātṛkā, [one recites]: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ*.

Ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, homage to the heart. (4) Iṃ caṃ (4) īṃ, svāhā to the head. (4) Uṃ ṭaṃ (4) Ūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock. (4) Eṃ taṃ (4) Aiṃ, huṃ to the armor. (4) Oṃ paṃ (4) Auṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. (4) Aṃ yaṃ (9) Aḥ, phaṭ to the weapon. Thus is the six-limbed [mantra].
Having performed the placement of the mantras on the two hands from the thumbs to the palms, one should also place them on the six limbs beginning with the heart.
Then follows the meditation (dhyāna).
Therein, first, having meditated upon subtle form, one should place the internal *mātṛkā*. It is as follows:

The sky [letter *ha*] is the pericarp with the letters *da*, *au*, *ra*, and *sa* as its filaments; it possesses the pairs of vowels as its throbbing stamens, and within its petals are the three groups of consonants (*ya-śal*, *a-kaca-ṭa-pa-ta-sa-ha*) in their respective order.

O Lord whose hand holds the plough, who is the refuge for those seeking protection, whose eyes are joined with the earth, and who dwells within the city of the body—may the lotus of your complexion, situated upon your head, destroy the poison of disease and grant purification. (1)
Thus, having meditated upon the lotus of letters in the aperture of Brahma.
Having heard the sound from the mūlādhāra, the kuṇḍalinī energy is awakened.
It blazes like glowing embers, having the nature of subtle light.
Having the form of lightning, she touches the crown-lotus from the root-support (mūlādhāra).
Touched by her, the lotus [on his head] became a mass of nectar in its very essence.
The letters of the alphabet, having emerged from the body, proceed through the channel of the suṣumṇā.
Having thus meditated on all those who remain pervading [the body], one should install them.
Having thus meditated upon her subtle form, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).

There, for the sake of purification, one should meditate on a sixteen-petaled lotus facing upward; then, upon its petals, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, one should assign the sixteen vowels: *aṃ namaḥ*, *āṃ namaḥ*, and so forth. Then, in the heart, one should meditate on the *anāhata* wheel as a twelve-petaled lotus, in the same manner.

One should place the twelve syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, preceded by the *praṇava* and the *tritārā* and ending with *namaḥ*, in clockwise order. Then, having meditated upon the *maṇipūraka* cakra at the navel as a ten-petaled lotus, one should place the ten syllables beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha* on its petals as before. Then...

Having meditated upon the Svādhiṣṭhāna cakra as a six-petaled lotus at the base of the liṅga, one should assign the six syllables beginning with *ba* and ending with *la* to its petals as before. Then, having meditated upon a four-petaled lotus at the Mūlādhāra, one should assign the four syllables beginning with *va* and ending with *sa* to its petals as previously described.
Then,
having meditated upon the *ājñācakra* as a two-petaled lotus between the eyebrows,
one should place the syllables *ha* and *kṣa* on its two petals as before. Having thus performed the internal *mātṛkā* placement (*nyāsa*), [one performs] the external *mātṛkā* placement.
One should perform [this]. Thus ends the internal placement of the *mātṛkās* (*antarmātṛkānyāsa*). As for the external placement (*bahirnyāsa*), therein is the visualization (*dhyāna*), as follows:
[One should meditate on the Goddess] whose face, arms, feet, belly, chest, and body are fashioned from the distinctions of the fifty letters;
who possesses a radiant matted lock (*kaparda*) adorned with the crescent moon; and who has the luster of the moon, jasmine, and a white cloud.

I bow to that Bhāratī, who holds a rosary, a water-pot, a lotus, and a book in her excellent hands; who has three eyes; who is seated upon a lotus; who is radiant; who possesses full breasts and hips; and who is free from all defects. (1)
The visualization of the weapons begins from the upper right hand and extends to the lower right hand.
The book written by thought—having meditated upon this in the previously mentioned lotus of letters, one should perform the placement (nyāsa). First, therein:

Having uttered the entire Mātṛkā beginning with *hsauṃḥ aṃ āṃ* and so forth, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) three times from the head down to the feet, ending with *hsauḥ namaḥ*. These syllables—*oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*—are to be understood as being used everywhere at the beginning of the ritual placements (*nyāsa*). On the head: *(4) aṃ namaḥ*. On the circumference of the mouth: *(4) āṃ namaḥ*. In the right eye: *(4) iṃ*...
*Namaḥ*. To the left eye: (4) *īṃ namaḥ*. To the right ear: (4) *uṃ namaḥ*. To the left ear: (4) *ūṃ namaḥ*. To the right nostril: (4) *ṛṃ namaḥ*. To the left nostril: (4) *ṝ namaḥ*.
To the right cheek: (4) ...

Ḷṃ namaḥ | On the left cheek: Ḹṃ namaḥ | On the upper lip: (4) Eṃ namaḥ | On the lower lip: (4) Aiṃ namaḥ | On the row of upper teeth: (4) Oṃ namaḥ | On the row of lower teeth: (4) Auṃ namaḥ | On the head: (4) Aṃ namaḥ | On the tongue: (4) Aḥ namaḥ | At the base of the right arm: (4) Kaṃ namaḥ |
*Namaḥ* to *khaṃ* at the right elbow; *namaḥ* to *gaṃ* at the right wrist;

*namaḥ* to *ghaṃ* at the base of the right fingers; *namaḥ* to *uṃḥ* at the tips of the right fingers. In this same manner, one should assign the [consonant] group to the left arm’s root, elbow, wrist, the bases of the fingers, and their tips. (Right...)

Then one should place the *ṭa*-group on the left side, the back, the navel, and the abdomen; then on the root of the right thigh, the knee, the ankle, and the base and tips of the fingers; then on the root of the left thigh, the knee, the ankle, and the base and tips of the fingers. [One should place them] on the right and left sides, the back, the navel, and the abdomen.
One should place the *va* group. Then, one should place the *ya* group on the heart, the right shoulder, the hump [of the spine], and the left shoulder.

Then, one should place the *śa* group on both hands starting from the heart, on both feet starting from the heart, on the navel starting from the heart, and in the *brahmarandhra* starting from the heart. This is the placement (*nyāsa*) of the pure *mātṛkā*. [The same applies to] the pure [vowels] joined with the *bindu*.

That which is adorned with the *hṛllekhā* along with the *visarga*, likewise encased by the *bālā*, and similarly adorned by the supreme *śrīvidyā*; he who knows how to join this hundred-fold placement (*nyāsa*) through both ascent and descent, as well as the two *haṃsas*, is indeed the creator of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all worlds. (1)
Regarding this, although the letters are pure, the inclusion of the *bindu* is for the purpose of joining them with vitality (*vīrya*); such is the tradition.
Now follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* accompanied by the *bindu*.
In this regard, the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as before. There is, however, a specific distinction in the visualization (*dhyāna*), which is as follows:
I worship her who has three eyes, who bestows knowledge, and who holds in her hands a rosary of beads, a young deer, a raised axe, and a magical lore.
Bow down to the Mistress of Colors, who rests upon a red lotus, whose crown is the crescent moon, and who is bent by the weight of her breasts. (1)
One should perform the visualization of the weapons starting from the lower right hand and ending with the lower left hand:
the *vidyā* (scripture), the book, and the *ṭaṅka* (a specific type of weapon). Having thus visualized them within the lotus of the letters, one should install them as follows:
*kṣaṃ namaḥ*, from the heart up to the *brahmarandhra* (the aperture at the crown of the head). (4)

From the heart to the navel: *laṃ namaḥ*, and so forth; up to the head: *aṃ namaḥ*. One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on those respective locations in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*). This is the placement of the *bindu-mātṛkā*.
Now follows the placement (nyāsa) of the Visarga-Mātṛkā.

In this regard, everything from the seer (ṛṣi) and so forth up to the visualization (dhyāna) is exactly as in the Śuddha-Mātṛkā. The specific distinction in the placement lies in the fact that the syllables are accompanied by the visarga. Thus ends the placement of the Visarga-Mātṛkā.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consists of the *mātṛkā* along with the nasal bindu and the visarga.
In this regard, the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other elements are exactly as in the case of the pure *mātṛkā*. However, there is a specific distinction in the visualization (*dhyāna*).
Thus: [one should meditate on the deity] with three eyes, adorned with vermilion and garments of desire...
Holding a rosary, a deer fawn, and a lotus.
One should also meditate upon the Blessed Lady standing at his side, possessing a golden luster, holding a book and a rosary in her lotus-like hands. (1)
One should meditate on the weapons of Śiva starting from the lower left hand up to the upper left hand;
for Śakti, however, [they are] on the two hands beginning with the left. Having thus meditated, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*). It is as follows:

At the right ankle (4): *ḍaṃ* namaḥ. At the base of the fingers (4): *ḍhaṃ* namaḥ. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the very locations of the pure Mātṛkā letters, beginning with the Praṇava and the three Tārās (4) and ending with *kṣaṃ* namaḥ, [one should proceed] from the head downwards on the right side, beginning with *aṃ* namaḥ and ending with *ṭhaṃ* namaḥ.

One should place [the letters] ending with the knees in the very locations of the pure Mātṛkā. Thus is the placement of the Mātṛkā consisting of the Bindu, Visarga, and the [vowels], which constitutes the form of the state (sthiti-rūpa).
Next is the placement of the Mātṛkā beginning with Hṛllekhā.

In this regard, Śakti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), and the Mother Sarasvatī, whose nature is Hṛllekhā, is the deity (*devatā*). Having thus recollected the seer and the other [components] and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): (4) *Aṃ Kaṃ* (4) *Āṃ Hrāṃ*, salutation to the heart (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*). (4) *Iṃ Caṃ* (4) *Īṃ Hrīṃ*, svāhā to the head (*śirase svāhā*). (4) *Uṃ Ṭaṃ* (4) *Ūṃ Hruṃ*, [salutation] to the tuft of hair (*śikhāyai*).

*Vaṣaṭ*. (4) *Aiṃ taṃ* (4) *Aiṃ Hraiṃ Kavacāya Huṃ*. (4) *Oṃ Paṃ* (4) *Auṃ Hrauṃ Netratrayāya Vauṣaṭ*. (4) *Aṃ Yaṃ* (9) *Aḥ Hraḥ Astrāya Phaṭ*. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the hands. Then follows the meditation (*dhyāna*).

The sixfold placement is also twofold, distinguished as the former and the latter. The latter is also threefold.

The sixfold imposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) consists of the Great Sixfold Imposition (*mahāṣoḍhānyāsa*), the Seed-Syllable Sixfold Imposition (*bījaṣoḍhānyāsa*), and the Mālinī Sixfold Imposition (*mālinyādi-ṣoḍhānyāsa*).

Among these, the former sixfold imposition pertains to all traditions (*sarvāmnāya*), while the latter sixfold imposition pertains specifically to the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*). The imposition of the Śrīcakra is likewise threefold.

This is due to the distinctions of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), and maintenance (*sthiti*). The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and purification (*karaśuddhi*) and so forth is also extensive, because specific types of placement such as those of Rati, Kāma, the fifty [syllables], Tripurā, and others are included therein by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).
Among these, first is the previously mentioned sixfold placement (*pūrvaṣoḍhānyāsa*). In that regard, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*).

Again, in the same manner, having filled the air through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī] and likewise retained it (*kuṃbhaka*), one should exhale in the same way; this is another method. No one has the right to perform ritual acts without breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
